text:
I've been seeing a lot of negativity around $CC lately. The price, Featured App rewards, what Super Validators are receiving, the marketing and the delays.

I get it. Nobody enjoys watching something they hold lose value, especially when they see others earning significant amounts of CC. Most of my crypto holdings are in CC.

But I think some perspective is needed.

Starting with Featured Apps, yes, the rewards can be generous. But there are requirements attached, including locking 5 million CC for non issuers or 25 million CC for asset issuers.

Then there's the work of building and running the product. Developers, infrastructure, support and ongoing improvements. I don't know what every team has spent, but none of that is free.

The rewards aren't the same for every project either. Featured App status doesn't automatically mean collecting millions of CC. The product a team builds and the qualifying network activity it generates matter.

If someone builds something useful, attracts users and contributes meaningful activity to Canton, I have no issue with them being rewarded.

There are already over 100 apps participating in the Featured App rewards system, and I expect that number to grow significantly over the coming years.

As more apps gain Featured App status and attract activity, I expect competition for those rewards to increase, with more projects earning a share. That doesn't mean every app will earn an equal amount, but I don't expect today's distribution to stay the same as the ecosystem grows.

Some of the people who built early are benefiting from being early. That's true, and I don't see that as a bad thing. They put time and resources into building something before knowing how it would turn out.

Does that mean every reward is justified or nothing needs adjusting? Of course not. But earning substantial rewards doesn't automatically mean a project is doing something wrong either.

Super Validators also have responsibilities and commitments to meet. Some of their reward allocations depend on milestones and contributions to the network. Not everything they do is necessarily visible to the average CC holder, and some information is confidential.

I think that context matters when discussing what they're receiving.

And let's be honest about my own experience too.

I've been involved since the early days of CC, and there was a period when I earned quite a lot for doing very little. Quite literally. I benefited from that myself.

It was great while it lasted, but was that ever going to be sustainable forever? Of course not.

I think it's only fair to acknowledge that when talking about rewards going to other people.

Another thing I keep coming back to is how young Canton's retail ecosystem still is.

People keep comparing Canton to established blockchain ecosystems that have had years to attract developers, build communities, launch applications and work through problems.

How much are we realistically expecting in such a short period?

I don't expect Canton to have the same depth of applications, tools and communities as ecosystems that have spent years developing them. I want to see progress, but I also want to be realistic about how long this takes.

There are new applications, tools and infrastructure being built, and plenty more being worked on in the background.

When I see teams spending their time and money building on Canton, that means something to me.

Why are all these people choosing to build here?

Clearly, they see an opportunity. That doesn't guarantee they'll succeed, but people generally don't invest significant time and resources into something unless they believe there's potential.

Canton isn't perfect, and I don't need to pretend it is to remain bullish.

There are things that can improve, and some of the criticism is warranted. But I also think Yuval and the wider team deserve credit for the effort they're making.

The founders are active, regularly joining livestreams, interviews and discussions, and engaging with people on X. I genuinely think they're doing a good job of making themselves available to the community.

Could communication improve in some areas? Absolutely. But I also think it's important to recognise the effort already being made.

CIPs are another part of that ongoing improvement. They exist to propose changes, address problems and improve how the network operates.

I'd rather see things constantly being reviewed and improved than have anyone pretend everything is already perfect.

And I don't expect every timeline to be exact. Sometimes things take longer than planned. I'd rather something be delivered properly than rushed just to hit a date.

Yuval has also spoken about doing more for the community, which I think is great. I'm looking forward to seeing what comes of that.

Again, these things take time.

On the investment side, my approach hasn't really changed.

I bought Tesla, Amazon and Meta shares early. I wasn't on X complaining about every marketing decision, every mistake or every time the share price dropped.

I invested because I believed in those companies and their long term potential.

There were ups and downs, periods of uncertainty, bad decisions and times when things weren't looking particularly good.

But I had conviction in my investments and was prepared to ride through those periods.

Look at Nvidia as another example.

Do you think everyone who invested in Nvidia years ago was happy with every single decision the company made? Every mistake, every setback, every drop in the share price?

Of course not.

Every company makes mistakes. Every company has things it needs to improve. Some make terrible decisions along the way.

Why should Canton be any different?

Why is every decision, every delay and every price movement scrutinised as though it's the end of the world?

Some of that scrutiny is absolutely warranted, and I'm not suggesting otherwise.

But let's apply some perspective and hold Canton to reasonable standards, just as we would with any other investment.

And before anyone says it, yes, buying shares in an established company is very different from investing in a crypto token. The risks are different, and I'm not suggesting Canton will follow the same path as any of those companies.

I'm talking about the mindset behind investing.

I want to understand what I'm buying, why I believe in it and what would make me change my mind. I don't want my entire opinion of an investment to depend on whether the price is green or red that week.

And right now, the positives I see in Canton far outweigh the negatives. That's my current assessment, and that's why I'm comfortable staying invested. If those reasons no longer hold up, I'll reassess.

There's also the speculative side of crypto.

Let's be real, a lot of investment in this space is driven by speculation. Hype, narratives and expectations about what something could become, rather than what it has actually achieved.

And I don't think Canton has really attracted that same level of speculative interest from retail yet.

Will that change? I'd like to think so.

As more people discover Canton, more applications launch and the ecosystem continues to grow, hopefully that interest will follow.

I'm already seeing Canton mentioned more regularly across X, more people learning about the network and more projects getting involved.

Compare that to where things were not so long ago.

But I also understand why people are cautious.

Nearly everyone in crypto has been burned at some point. People have lost money, invested in projects that promised everything and delivered nothing, and watched entire ecosystems disappear.

It takes time to build trust, especially among retail investors who have been through all of that.

You can't expect everyone to suddenly discover Canton, trust the network, invest their money and become long term supporters overnight.

That trust needs to be earned.

And growing awareness doesn't automatically mean the price of CC will go up. Eventually, interest needs to translate into real adoption and sustainable network activity.

That's something I want to see develop over time.

Most of my crypto holdings are in CC, alongside a few other Canton ecosystem tokens. I'm holding, earning yield and watching how things develop.

Of course I want CC to go up. I'm hardly enjoying the dips. But I didn't buy expecting a straight line up, and I'm certainly not expecting a 10x within the next month.

I'm more interested in what Canton looks like in two, three or five years than what happens to the chart next week.

If you can't handle a price dip, or you're already fed up because your investment hasn't done a 10x, maybe CC isn't the right investment for you.

There's always a memecoin being hyped as the next 100x somewhere. 

I'm not here for a quick flip. I'm taking a longer view and I'm prepared to sit through difficult periods while my reasons for investing still hold up.

And this is probably the most important point.

If you can't handle losses, or losing money would seriously affect your daily life, be very careful about how much you invest. That applies to stocks and even more so to crypto.

As bullish as I am on Canton and CC, even I understand the risks involved. Nothing is guaranteed, and I could be wrong.

If you're investing for the long term, you need to be prepared for the ups and downs. If you're trading and looking for quick gains, that's a completely different approach, and CC might not be what you're looking for.

What I don't agree with is treating every setback as proof that the whole network has failed, any more than I agree with treating every announcement as proof that CC is about to take off.

I can be bullish on Canton and still disagree with decisions being made. I can question rewards, want better communication and still recognise the effort going into the network.

I don't think those positions contradict each other.

Look at the projects being built, the applications being launched, the institutions involved, the infrastructure being developed and the people spending their time and money trying to grow the ecosystem.

There's a lot happening, and much of it takes place without the average CC holder necessarily seeing it.

As cliche as it sounds, I genuinely believe we're still early in Canton's development.

Not early in the sense that everyone is guaranteed to make money by buying CC today, but early in terms of how much of the ecosystem still needs to be built and how much adoption still needs to happen.

There are challenges ahead, things that need improving and plenty that could go wrong.

But there's also a lot to be positive about.

And I think it's worth explaining why I spend so much time involved with Canton in the first place.

The goal with Canton Army and CantonNews has always been to educate people, promote the ecosystem and support the projects building within it.

That's what we're here to do.

We want to help people understand Canton, discover new projects, learn how things work and stay informed about what's happening across the network.

We'll share the information, highlight opportunities and showcase what teams are building. What you choose to do with that information is entirely up to you.

We're not here to give financial advice, convince anyone to buy CC or push people into buying other tokens or memecoins.

That's never been our goal.

We believe in Canton, which is why we dedicate so much time to covering the ecosystem and supporting the people building here.

And you won't see us crying on X every time the price drops.

Of course we'd prefer the price to be going up, but our long term conviction hasn't changed. We'll continue supporting Canton, helping projects get exposure and growing the community to the best of our ability, regardless of what the chart looks like on any given day.

For me, there's enough progress and potential to remain invested, keep building and give the ecosystem time to develop.

I don't expect everything to go perfectly, but the positives still heavily outweigh the negatives in my view.

And just to be clear, this isn't a post trying to convince anyone to buy CC, and it isn't a prediction that the price will go up.

It's simply my take on the current state of Canton and CC, why I remain invested and why I'm prepared to give it time.

Everyone has their own expectations, investment strategies and appetite for risk. You might disagree with some of what I've said, and that's absolutely fine.

I don't claim to have all the answers, and I'm certainly not saying Canton gets everything right.

I just think there's a much bigger picture here than the daily price movements.

That's my perspective, and it's why I'm still bullish on Canton for the long term.

author: BillAckman
quoted_text:
A Stanford student got reported for academic misconduct last semester.

His research paper was so good his professor assumed he bought it.

The academic integrity hearing lasted 3 hours.

Here's what happened in that room.

The panel asked him to explain his methodology from scratch. He opened his laptop, pulled up https://t.co/LaaeCA6T1b, and started rebuilding the entire paper live in front of them.

First he fed it his raw notes and asked: "You are a research methodology expert. Here are my raw notes. Identify the 3 strongest arguments buried in this data, rank them by originality, and show me exactly where each one challenges or extends existing literature."

The professors went quiet.

Then he ran: "Now simulate a hostile peer reviewer with a PhD in this field. Generate every serious objection they would raise against my thesis. Then tell me which objections actually have merit and which ones I can dismantle."

One professor leaned forward and asked him to stop so she could write down the prompt.

He kept going. "Take my weakest argument and steelman it harder than I did. Show me what it would look like if it were airtight. Then tell me what I'd need to prove to get it there."

Then the one that ended the hearing. "You are my thesis advisor. I have 24 hours before submission. Read this draft and tell me the single change that would move this from a B+ to an A. Be brutal."

He walked them through how he'd used that last output to rewrite his conclusion three times until it held up under every objection in the room.

What took most PhD candidates 6 months of back-and-forth with advisors, he was doing in real-time inside a single workflow.

The panel didn't just clear him.

They gave him the highest grade in the department's history and asked him to present the workflow to faculty.

The irony is beautiful. The paper looked too good to be human because he'd found a way to think harder than most humans bother to.

That's not cheating. That's the new ceiling.

text:
I disagree with @EthanDeFi_ here. No one is criticizing Morpho for being decentralized.

Yes, Morpho Blue is immutable, but the @Morpho team still runs the main app, decides which curators and vaults get listed, and can delist them for risk at its discretion.

That’s curation. It shapes where users put their money.

So when a curator vault blows up, “the protocol can’t intervene” only covers half the stack. The other half is a choice not to.

Isolated markets also mean isolated liquidity, which is one reason we consistently see the largest lending operations happen on @Aave, not Morpho.

Morpho has proven to be great lending infrastructure, but the criticism was never decentralization: it's using decentralization as cover to avoid protecting users.

text:
The argument for Binance's insolvency 🧵

Binance claims to have replaced 90% of the $6.3 billion lost in the hack

But how do we know Binance isn't borrowing billions against customer deposits to cover the losses?

Binance is a private company operating through a complex corporate structure across multiple jurisdictions

It is largely unregulated and does not publicly disclose its complete audited balance sheet or liabilities the same way that Coinbase for example does

This makes its "Proof of Reserves" meaningless as evidence of solvency

Binance could theoretically pledge customer assets as collateral while continuing to report those same assets in its reserves

And if Binance collapses then secured creditors could have priority over depositors and potentially recover billions before customers receive anything

This is precisely the kind of opacity that allowed FTX to conceal its financial condition until it was too late

It's important to remember that CZ is a convicted felon and these people lie to our faces about simple things like "we don't charge listing fees"

No matter how many times they tell you that your funds are safe they are in fact obviously not

CZ and Binance cannot be trusted

There is zero upside to leaving your funds in Binance right now

BREAKING: Inside Starcloud, the $2.3B Startup Putting Data Centers in Space

FACTORY TOUR - Redmond, WA

Primes quoted them $75M-$100M to build their first data center in space. They did it for $2.5M.

In just 21 months, Starcloud is one of the fastest companies to go from founding to orbit.

With $450M in total funding from Manhattan West, Nvidia, Cisco, Benchmark & EQT, the team walks me through their mission for AI in space.

I toured the new HQ w/ CEO @PhilipJohnston + co-founders @EzraFeilden & @AdiOltean

AI compute on Earth is limited by power & permitting. @Starcloud_ is moving it to orbit, where solar power is nearly constant. Philip says the dawn-dusk orbit alone could fit about 10 TW of compute, roughly 20x the entire US power grid. Once launch costs fall below $500/kg, he says compute in space will be cheaper than on the ground.

From Starcloud 1, Starcloud 2, to Starcloud 3, we saw: 

Tracking Starcloud 1 live in orbit, circling Earth every 90 minutes at 17,000 mph with the first Nvidia H100 in space.

Co-Founder & Chief Engineer Adi Oltean walks through Starcloud 2 as the team fires the latches that deploy its 120 ft solar wingspan. It launches in January with 100x the power of Starcloud 1. 

Co-Founder & CTO Ezra Feilden shows the 16-ton secondhand vibe table. The team bought it for $200K, instead of paying $1.5M & waiting 2 years for a new one, they rebuilt it over a weekend.

Engineering Manager Bailey Montaño leak checks the ion thruster after vibe. Bailey designed the radiators, which have 10x less mass & cost 500x less per watt than the ISS’s.

The Vulnpocalypse - Good News and Bad News

- The bad news is we are inundated with new vulnerabilities due to the increased volumes discovered by AI tooling.

- The good news is many organizations are starting to handle this with increased speed, prioritization, and existing methods of defense in depth.

- The bad news is there are also many organizations not doing this, and worse, are sitting on a whole ton of software, configuration, and structural/policy vulnerabilities from prior years.

- The good news is many of these targets have not been exploited due to attacker’s resource constraints.

- The bad news is that this might not hold as attackers industrialize their capabilities to turn more targets of opportunity into actual victims.

- The good news is, apart from scams, crypto/Web3, and some parts of the ransomware kill chain, it appears that such industrialization is not helping monetization (yet).

- The bad news is attackers are an innovative bunch and not likely to give up and go set up a bakery, or go back to drug dealing. Besides, chaos may still ensue as agent swarms simply exploit vulnerabilities anyway.

- The good news is defenders can use all this AI capability for defense. We are seeing the potential that many significant code bases will have dramatically lower vulnerabilities levels than ever before due to the “deep cleaning” (h/t @argvee) with the very same tools we are concerned attackers will use.

- The bad news is getting a code base “clean” doesn’t mean the updated packaged software will arrive quickly in all the places where attacks will target.

The good news is……..?

At @web3summit 2026, people bought coffee, explored apps and deployed smart contracts. Several temporary networks supported those activities, but most attendees did not need to know which chain handled each task.

In its article, @paritytech connects that experience to the thinking behind Polkadot Products.

The approach addresses practical questions:

• Why should every developer rebuild the same tools? Shared services for identity, signing and payments can reduce the work needed before a team can focus on its application.
• Can apps feel more consistent across devices? Trinity explores a shared environment for mobile, desktop and the web, with applications using a common interface for those services.
• Does recognising a person require knowing who they are? Humanity focuses on establishing that someone is a unique person without revealing their identity.
• How easily can someone test an idea? At the Summit, Playground let participants modify working prototypes and deploy them to a temporary network.
The article describes work in progress, not a finished platform. It also acknowledges that getting started still needs to become easier for new users.
For technology built around people, ease of use is only part of the goal. The harder question is whether we can make software simpler without asking people to give up privacy, ownership or choice.

Less complexity should mean products that give people greater agency rather than platforms greater control.

text:
Slavery was an evil in which people from every continent and region participated. We should be honest about the whole history, not select the parts that are politically convenient today, especially given Britain's leading role in ending the transatlantic slave trade.

If Caribbean countries are asking Britain for a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, will they also be asking the same of the descendants of African kingdoms, rulers and merchants who captured, sold and profited from the trade?

On demands for reparations, whether through cash or debt relief, we have been down this track before. Twenty-five years ago, Jubilee 2000, Drop the Debt and Make Poverty History argued that cancelling the debts of poorer countries would give them a fresh start. More than $100 billion of debt was eventually written off, but many of those countries have since built up even bigger debts. Labour are already spending too much on Britain's welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare. 

There is no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born. And I have even less patience for political elites in commonwealth countries who don’t know how to make their own citizens prosperous now looking for another opportunity to blame Britain.

As Prime Minister, Andy Burnham should be Britain’s greatest defender. Instead, he is writing articles saying we need to confront our history (as if we haven't done enough of that) and considering another formal historical apology. Tony Blair already expressed Britain’s deep sorrow and regret for our role in the slave trade nearly twenty years ago. There is no need to do so again. 

This is all another navel-gazing distraction. The Commonwealth should be looking forward, not endlessly backwards. That means economic partnerships to make us all richer and deeper military and security cooperation against common threats. If every Commonwealth summit becomes an exercise in presenting Britain with demands for cash then we need to start asking if it is worth the effort.

Hedge funds just hit the panic button harder than at any time in the last ten years. Here is why that is good news for you.

Morgan Stanley tracks the total money its hedge fund clients have bet on stocks. When that total drops sharply, it means funds are being forced to cut positions, usually because their losses hit a limit. In the last 2 days, it fell 7.8%, a bigger unwind than the Covid crash, the GameStop squeeze, or the 2016 and 2018 selloffs.

Every time this number fell past 6% (2016, 2018 twice, 2020, 2021, 2025), the S&P 500 bottomed within a week or two and was higher one, three and six months later. Six out of six.

The reason is simple. Once the forced sellers have sold, there is nobody left to push prices down. Those same funds then have to buy back in, and that buying has powered every rebound in the table.

Ethereum: finality needs 2/3 stake. Without it finality stalls; inactivity leak drains offline stake until active validators regain supermajority and finalize. 16h is short; recovery automatic unless split lasts weeks (then possible permanent forks needing social resolution).

Protocols themselves are the plan; no extra global fix required. Ops practices (multi-path nodes, monitoring, freezes) handle the rest.

Very low chance next year of a clean multi-region isolation lasting hours—internet routing is highly redundant.

text: V8's optimizing JIT (TurboFan/Maglev) does speculative optimization from type feedback. From there JIT spraying or Wasm jump-table corruption yields RCE. Roughly 45% of V8 CVEs and over half of in-the-wild Chrome exploits target this path. Hardware acceleration adds a separate GPU-process surface for sandbox escapes. Disabling both shrinks the dominant attack vectors.

text:
Everyone's talking about peptides now.

3 of the top 10 best-selling drugs of 2025 were peptides.

Here's the origin story:

In 1901, Emil Fischer's research group in Berlin synthesized the first free dipeptide, two amino acids joined together. A year later, he gave the name "peptide" to compounds formed by linking amino acids.

In January 1922, Leonard Thompson, a boy weighing a mere 65 pounds, hovered between life and death in Toronto. Back then, it often came down to death by diabetes or death by starvation.

The first injection was impure and had little effect. Then James Collip improved the purity of the extract. His records read: "The boy became brighter, more active, looked better and said he felt stronger."

Insulin became the first therapeutic peptide.

But it all came from animals. By 1981, one pound of insulin required 8,000 pounds of glands from 23,500 animals, only enough to treat 750 patients for one year.

Making peptides in a lab was truly a heroic task. Even at a 90% yield in each step, a 100-step chain would end with 0.003%.

And they didn't last. Digestion tends to break peptides down, and human GLP-1 breaks down within minutes.

The fixes took decades.

In 1963, Bruce Merrifield attached the growing peptide chain to a resin bead, eventually raising the yield in each step to 99.5%.

In 1982, the FDA approved human insulin made by bacteria.

In the early 1990s, John Eng found a peptide in Gila monster venom that closely resembled human GLP-1 but lasted far longer in the body. In 2005, it became the first GLP-1 drug.

Today, 11% of U.S. adults take GLP-1 medications for weight loss.

Everyone's talking about peptides now because, 125 years later, they can be made in a lab, in large amounts, and built to last.

text:
A HUGE part of this market selloff is being driven by one of the biggest hedge fund deleveraging events we've seen in over a decade.

According to Morgan Stanley Prime Brokerage data, hedge funds have reduced their gross exposure by roughly 7.8% from its recent peak. That's the largest drawdown in this dataset going back to 2016, even surpassing the deleveraging we saw during the COVID crash in 2020. For those unfamiliar, deleveraging basically means hedge funds are reducing risk by unwinding positions, cutting leverage, and selling assets. And here's where things get interesting because when these funds start taking losses, they often have to sell positions to bring their risk back under control. That selling pushes prices lower, which can trigger even more selling across other funds. This creates a domino effect where stocks can get absolutely hammered regardless of how strong their underlying businesses are. A fund might be bullish on AI infrastructur but if it's facing losses elsewhere or needs to reduce leverage, it may have no choice but to sell those positions anyway.

And that's a big reason why we're seeing so much volatility across the technology sector right now. Concerns about AI spending, financing, and valuations have already pressured some of the most crowded trades on Wall Street. Add massive hedge fund deleveraging on top of that, and you have a situation where selling creates more selling, even without additional bad news. The important distinction here is that this isn't necessarily a reflection of deteriorating company fundamentals. Some companies are genuinely facing challenges but others are getting caught in a broader liquidation cycle simply because institutions need to reduce exposure. The interesting part is what happens once this selling pressure starts to fade. If hedge funds finish reducing their exposure while earnings and underlying demand remain strong, some of these beaten down stocks could recover sharply as liquidity returns and investors rebuild positions. That doesn't mean we've necessarily reached the bottom. But I think it's important to understand that a significant part of this selloff appears to be driven by positioning and risk reduction, not just a sudden collapse in the long term AI investment thesis. https://t.co/bj8SwNPOeF

"I worry more about the pure play neocloud companies that are a bit like highly levered real estate developers playing a theme. I think they’re much more at risk. They’re much more sensitive to the cost of capital."

"But you have, I mean, SpaceX, Elon on the earnings call gave some projections for how many gigawatts of data centers he was going to open. If he meets his objective, he might have to borrow a trillion dollars of capital."

"So, you have companies competing at sovereign levels for debt. And the result is, you know, this massive, you know, more and more supply of debt. So, I don’t see a world in which, you know, there’s a dramatic, you know, there’s a lot of demand for capital and a finite supply. So, I think that makes rates persistently high.”

Your agent's approval screen can show the right tool and the right arguments, and the server still picks the price.

This morning I went through a draft standard where a person signs off each tool call their agent makes. The approval covers the server, the tool and the arguments. With x402 paid tools, the price and the payee only come back from the server after the first call, and the agent pays on the retry. So the person never sees the price, and the approval passes at any price.

If your agent pays for tools, make the approval cover the amount and the payee, and check it where the payment gets signed 🫡

BREAKING: Inside Starcloud, the $2.3B Startup Putting Data Centers in Space

FACTORY TOUR - Redmond, WA

Primes quoted them $75M-$100M to build their first data center in space. They did it for $2.5M.

In just 21 months, Starcloud is one of the fastest companies to go from founding to orbit.

With $450M in total funding from Manhattan West, Nvidia, Cisco, Benchmark & EQT, the team walks me through their mission for AI in space.

I toured the new HQ w/ CEO @PhilipJohnston + co-founders @EzraFeilden & @AdiOltean

AI compute on Earth is limited by power & permitting. @Starcloud_ is moving it to orbit, where solar power is nearly constant. Philip says the dawn-dusk orbit alone could fit about 10 TW of compute, roughly 20x the entire US power grid. Once launch costs fall below $500/kg, he says compute in space will be cheaper than on the ground.

From Starcloud 1, Starcloud 2, to Starcloud 3, we saw: 

Tracking Starcloud 1 live in orbit, circling Earth every 90 minutes at 17,000 mph with the first Nvidia H100 in space.

Co-Founder & Chief Engineer Adi Oltean walks through Starcloud 2 as the team fires the latches that deploy its 120 ft solar wingspan. It launches in January with 100x the power of Starcloud 1. 

Co-Founder & CTO Ezra Feilden shows the 16-ton secondhand vibe table. The team bought it for $200K, instead of paying $1.5M & waiting 2 years for a new one, they rebuilt it over a weekend.

Engineering Manager Bailey Montaño leak checks the ion thruster after vibe. Bailey designed the radiators, which have 10x less mass & cost 500x less per watt than the ISS’s. 

In the fab shop, Ezra shows the Starcloud 3 demonstrator, a 2-ton, 235 kW vehicle that fits 50 to a Starship. 

Camilo Lopez cuts stainless on the laser cutter. 

Engineering Operations Lead Miguel Rivera, formerly of Helion Energy, teaches me to MIG weld.

The tour ends in the new campus, about 100,000 sqft built to produce 100 satellites a week toward an 88,000-satellite constellation.

爬虫项目：Scrapling 已经 90K 🌟了啊！猛啊！！

一直关注着，回头一年快 100K 了，这就能证明一些事情了。。

它能帮你自动从网站上收集资料、提取信息的开源工具，还可以接入 AI，让 AI 帮你完成这些工作。

举个电商应用例子：

你想研究 20 个同行网站上的产品价格、卖点和用户评价。
以前，你需要一个个打开网站，复制内容，再交给 AI 整理。

现在，可以让 Scrapling 批量获取这些网页上的信息，再让 AI 分析、比较，最后整理成表格。

我认为下面几个场景最有实际价值：

1. 自媒体选题和素材收集

比如让它收集指定博客、媒体网站上的文章标题、发布时间、正文，再交给 AI 寻找热门话题和选题方向。

2. 电商竞品调研

刚说过，也可以查竞品的评论数据。

3. 建立自己的 AI 知识库

把指定文档网站、教程网站的公开内容批量提取为 Markdown，供 AI 检索和分析。

4. 招聘和商业信息整理（有商业价值）

5. 给 AI Agent 增加网页信息采集能力

配置 MCP 后，支持该协议的 AI 工具可以调用 Scrapling 访问网页、提取指定内容，部分情况下还能操作浏览器。

Scrapling 针对网页结构发生一些变化后，它有机会重新找到要提取的内容，减少维护工作。

值得一试！

text:
Over the past two weeks iPhones have been publicly jailbroken more than once, and most people treated it as a bit of tech drama and scrolled on. I want to use it to talk about something that matters more to people in crypto: wiping an old iPhone, putting it in airplane mode and using it only to hold your seed phrase is not as safe as most people think. If it's an iPhone 11 or older, the problem lives in the chip, and no iOS update will fix it.

Quick recap of what happened. On October 16 at Hexacon in Paris, the Calif team jailbroke an iPhone 18 Pro running iOS 27.0.1 live on stage. The jailbreak survived a reboot, they had root, and they got past MIE, the hardware memory protection Apple added starting with the A19 specifically to stop spyware. In the same session they showed attacks that get in through a single click in Signal or iMessage. A week later, on the day iPhone Duo went on sale, they jailbroke that too. Apple shipped iOS 27.2 on October 26, and Calif says most of the bugs they used are now fixed. Then on October 30, Ikotas Labs, the Japanese team that just won Pwn2Own, posted that they had jailbroken 27.2 as well. Their video only shows swapped icons and the version number, though, so I'm treating it as unconfirmed for now.

For most people on a recent phone who keep it updated, none of this is a reason to panic. Before chains like these get patched, they usually sit with spyware vendors and forensics companies, and the odds of an ordinary person being specifically targeted are low. Update to 27.2 and you've done what you need to.

The people I actually want to warn are those using an old iPhone as a cold wallet. iPhone 4S through iPhone X have checkm8 in the BootROM, made public in 2019. This June, usbliter8 went public, covering the iPhone XS, XR, the 11 series and the 2nd-gen SE. The BootROM is boot code burned into the chip at the factory. Apple can't patch it with a software update, so these devices will carry the hole for as long as they exist. Exploiting it doesn't need a network either. Once someone has your phone in hand, they put it into DFU mode and plug in a custom USB board (the public research used a $5 Raspberry Pi Pico 2), and they can run their own code before iOS even boots. Airplane mode makes no difference here.

I don't want to overstate it. On models like the XS and 11, the BootROM bug alone won't hand over your seed phrase, because your passcode and the Secure Enclave are still in the way. The trouble is that these remaining layers are exactly where people tend to cut corners: a 6-digit passcode, an iOS version years out of date with a pile of public n-days, a short wallet app password. On some older models, forensic tools use bugs like this to brute-force the passcode. And if your wallet app encrypts the seed with nothing but a short password, once that encrypted file is copied off, the attacker can take it home and keep guessing offline, with no attempt limit. Old iOS versions also have a charging port problem. ChoiceJacking, published in 2025, lets a malicious charger pose as a keyboard and approve the data-access prompt for you. Apple only closed that in iOS 18.4.

One more thing about this kind of attack: when you get your phone back, nothing looks off. In security circles it's called an evil maid attack. A hotel room, a security check, lending your phone to someone to charge — any time it's out of your hands for a while, there's an opening. A lot of people only find out their phone was touched after their assets are already gone.

My advice:

1. Check which iPhone holds your seed phrase (Settings → General → About). If it's an iPhone 11 or older, move to a newer model before storing a seed on it.

2. If you've already stored one there, no need to panic. When you get a chance, generate a brand-new seed phrase in an environment you trust and move your assets over. It has to be a whole new seed. A fresh address under the old seed won't help.

3. If your phone has ever been out of your hands for a while, say held for inspection at a border, don't wait. Migrate as in step 2 as soon as you can.

4. Update your daily iPhone to iOS 27.2 (Settings → General → Software Update). If you haven't moved to 27 yet, install at least 26.7.2.

5. Switch to a long alphanumeric passcode (Settings → Face ID & Passcode → Change Passcode → Passcode Options). A 6-digit PIN has only a million possible combinations. Make your wallet app password longer too.

6. Carry your own charger. Don't use public USB ports, random power banks or cables you don't know.

7. If you hold a lot or are likely to be targeted, consider turning on Lockdown Mode (Settings → Privacy & Security → Lockdown Mode). It blocks wired connections while the phone is locked.

8. Any "iOS 27 jailbreak download," or any tutorial asking you to install a certificate or configuration profile, is a scam or malware. Neither Calif nor Ikotas has released any tools.

If you like using an iPhone as a cold wallet, go with a newer model and keep it on the latest iOS. There's no public BootROM exploit for the iPhone 12 or later, and if something does turn up, Apple can still fix it with an update. With really old devices, the risk sits in the chip itself, and updating iOS won't get you around it.

author: Tangem
quoted_text:
A screen makes your hardware wallet safer? Think again.

Recent security incidents tell a different story.

1. Ledger, October 2026 — Hardware Implant
A hidden hardware implant captured recovery phrases directly from the device’s screen and transmitted them over LTE. The Secure Element remained intact.

2. Ledger, August 2026 — Transaction Mismatch
A Clear Signing vulnerability allowed the transaction parameters displayed on the screen to differ from those actually signed.

3. Trezor, May 2026 — Hidden ETH Transfer
A Clear Signing flaw could hide an additional ETH transfer while displaying a routine token transaction.

What this shows:
A screen doesn’t guarantee you’re seeing everything you’re signing. And more hardware components can introduce more attack vectors.

Why Tangem doesn’t need a screen:
• Your phone displays transaction details through a security-hardened app.
• Multiple protection layers help defend against UI manipulation, malicious overlays, and runtime attacks.
• Private keys remain inside the secure chip.
• No screen, no battery, no unnecessary hardware complexity.

https://t.co/sIYShVL1cp

Security is about protecting the entire system, not just adding more components.

Financial Markets, not Prediction Markets, now suggest a split Congress, not a Democratic sweep.

The @goldmansachs Affordable Care Act (ACA) Basket (GSHLCACA) divided by the S&P 500 ex-AI (SPXXAI) vs. a Democratic Sweep Odds on @Kalshi.

The two series tracked closely from April through mid-October 2026, both rising as Democratic sweep odds climbed from ~40 to ~65+.

However, we are now seeing a stark divergence in the last two weeks.

The ACA ratio (black) peaked near 115 around Oct 14-16, then sold off hard to 106.41 -- a roughly 8-point drop. 

The Dem sweep odds (blue) held at 65-66 and actually ticked up slightly over the same window.

That decoupling is the signal, in my opinion.

Three probable reasons for the divergence:

1. Profit-taking / position unwind

The ACA basket had an outsized run (~+15% relative to ex-AI S&P since September). Institutions that rode the political trade are harvesting gains ahead of Nov 4 elections, regardless of current odds. I see this as a sensible but low probability.

2. Sweep odds vs. implementation risk

Kalshi House odds sit at ~91% Dem, Senate at ~64% Dem (Kalshi News, Oct 27-28). A full sweep is priced in on the House but the Senate is a coin flip with 36% GOP. Markets may be pricing the scenario where Dems win the House but not the Senate; ACA expansion stalls in a split Congress.

I see this as most likely.

3. $XLV flow context

Dark pool data shows heavy distribution on Oct 30 (buy ratio dropped to 0.30, strongest sell signal in the 20-day window). 
Options flow remains strongly bullish (put/call premium ratio 0.19), so there is a split:  institutional blocks distributing while options desks stay long vol into the election. That kind of conflict typically signals hedging, not conviction.

Also a sensible explanation, but again, seems less likely

In short, the ACA basket is repricing from a "full sweep, full expansion" multiple toward a "House only" multiple. 

Sweep odds have not moved, but the marginal value of the Senate seat is being discounted. 

The divergence is the market saying that a House win is in the price, Senate is the variable, and the trade already had a 15% run.

text:
Anthropic is about to go public as one of the most valuable companies in the world, and its debt is about to get rated junk.

The firm that told investors owns $9 billion of that debt, and it set the interest rate at junk levels from day one.

Sounds backwards until you see the rate. Blackstone's funds bought in at a yield above 10%. That's what lenders charge a borrower they think is risky, and Blackstone has been getting paid that premium since it wrote the check.

The way the deal works is kind of clever. Anthropic needs $63 billion worth of Google's AI chips. Instead of borrowing all that itself, a separate company buys the chips and rents them to Anthropic, and the rent pays the lenders back. Broadcom, which has a strong A rating, guarantees more than $42 billion of it. Only about $18 billion depends on Anthropic alone, and Blackstone took half of that.

You can actually see what Anthropic's own name costs to borrow against. In an earlier $35 billion chip deal led by Apollo, lenders charged 5.75% on the part Broadcom guaranteed and about 8.5% on the part riding on Anthropic.

Now do the math on Blackstone's slice. $9 billion at 10% instead of 5.75% comes to roughly $380 million a year in extra interest. Anthropic brought in $16.8 billion last quarter, which works out to about $183 million a day.

So the junk rating on that slice costs Anthropic about two days of revenue a year.

Why junk at all? Credit agencies mostly want to know whether your cash flow can cover your debt. When KBRA gave Anthropic a BB+ back in June, the highest junk rating there is, it had to work off a risk score because Anthropic never handed over its free cash flow or EBITDA. The analysts had to guess. Nobody hands out investment grade on a guess, least of all to a company planning $800 billion of compute spending through 2045.

Tesla was sitting on that exact rung not long ago. In October 2021 it became the first company worth $1 trillion with junk-rated debt. A year later S&P bumped it up from BB+ to investment grade.

Netflix is the longer version of the same playbook. It started selling junk bonds in 2009 and kept at it for more than a decade, borrowing to pay for the shows that built its subscriber base. S&P had it at B+, four notches deep in junk, as late as 2018. S&P rates it A now.

The part I'd actually watch is the structure. Most of this financing leans on Broadcom's balance sheet, and Broadcom's own filing says the business depends on Anthropic's continued commercial success. Revenue jumped from $11.5 billion to $16.8 billion in a single quarter. As long as that keeps going, BB is probably a pit stop on the way to investment grade. The scary version is growth stalling while $18 billion of debt sits on a company its own lenders already priced as junk.

The rating agencies are basically catching up to an interest rate Blackstone set on day one.

In the case of Lighter:

1. All data is verifiable - you don't have to trust the operator.  Withdraw your funds via escape hatch if Lighter stops operating. There are CLOBs for other products like spot/options where realtime settlement makes a difference, and it is synergistic via portfolio margin

2. Lighter can trivially offer privacy to traders by encrypting data (with the trader's public key) before it's posted to Ethereum. This does not affect the escape hatch. Position level privacy can be mandatory, opt-in, or opt-out. Trades, volume and open interest can remain public, verifiable info while individual trader positions remain hidden

3. No priority fees on Lighter. 

4. Combining onshore/offshore orderbooks is technically possible but that's up to the regulators.

5. Lighter matching engine is centralized and highly performant. There is no tradeoff between speed and security. If there is inefficiency, it is the cost of generating and publishing proofs of correct execution, which is low and continuing to drop quickly.

Further to my post about @NYSE working to bring @HyperliquidX onshore, major credit to @ChairmanSelig and the Trump administration for making all of this experimentation possible. 

There’s only one way of finding out if something is useful to the marketplace and I’m excited for us to find out. I do have some questions:

1. What is the benefit of trading perps on-chain on a regulated exchange? Isn’t the main benefit of trading on-chain to operate in a trustless (aka non-kyc’d) environment in order to minimize friction, and/or to be able to enter into atomic transactions in order to receive what you are buying in realtime? Since a perp is not an asset, that obviously isn’t helpful. 

2. @standuquesne - are you aware that if you trade on Hyperliquid, the world will be able to track your positions and trades in real time? Do you see that as a benefit?

3. Hyperliquid has priority fees - a mechanism that enables market participants to pay to see information first, or even prioritize orders in front of the queue. Is this consistent with CFTC core principles?

4. Will it be possible to combine the liquidity of the offshore order-book with the onshore order-book?

5. If not, wouldn’t it be better to list perps in a traditional (centralized) order-book on a regulated exchange and not have the inefficiencies that on-chain matching introduces?

text:
Remember when we warned the internet was going into LOCKDOWN?

October is almost over, and "Black October" has lived up to its name.

This is going to be a long one.

It started with PHP, the software behind roughly 7 in 10 websites.

On October 20, two critical flaws were revealed in it, letting attackers take over servers without logging in.

Within 2 hours, Cloudflare saw hundreds of thousands of attack attempts, and soon after, MILLIONS.

Governments in the UK, the Netherlands, France, Denmark and Finland took websites offline as a precaution.

On October 26, the US cyber agency CISA confirmed the flaws were being exploited and gave federal agencies three days to patch.

At the same time, a wave of data breaches hit, and Japan took the worst of it.

SourceNext exposed 22.5 MILLION records, Skyticket 14.6 MILLION, Capcom 11.8 MILLION and Burger King Japan 11.2 MILLION.

Denmark's population register was breached, exposing data on 8.8 MILLION people.

But the real thread running through Black October was AI.

Wall Street giants like JPMorgan and Schwab are now blocking outside AI agents, with Schwab's CEO saying a single agent can try to log in "30, 40, 50 times" a week.

Attackers also went after AI tools and AI keys, hijacking LiteLLM, downloaded 23 MILLION times a week, and breaching Railway, OpenCode and Fireworks AI.

Then came October 29.

Binance was hacked for $6.3 BILLION and has already covered 90%, with withdrawals set to reopen on November 1.

The same day, Polymarket paused trading after a compromised third party script drained about $2.7 MILLION from its users.

Bitcoin is down about 7% for October, heading for its second red October in a row, and Ethereum is down about 16%.

These stock markets turned blood red in October:

🇮🇩 Indonesia 🔻16.7%
🇰🇷 South Korea 🔻16.2%
🇧🇷 Brazil 🔻9.9%
🇨🇳 China 🔻6.3%
🇹🇼 Taiwan 🔻5.7%
🇭🇰 Hong Kong 🔻5.4%
🇺🇸 Nasdaq 🔻5.3%
🇸🇬 Singapore 🔻5.3%
🇯🇵 Japan 🔻5.2%
🇪🇸 Spain 🔻4%
🇮🇹 Italy 🔻3.6%
🇪🇺 Euro Stoxx 50 🔻2.2%
🇲🇾 Malaysia 🔻2.2%
🇻🇳 Vietnam 🔻1.5%
🇺🇸 S&P 500 🔻0.9%

Intel had its worst day since 1974, and Alphabet its worst since its 2004 IPO, losing about $482 BILLION.

Oil touched $110, and US inflation climbed to 3.7%.

October tested the internet, global markets and crypto all at once.

All three took heavy hits, and all three are still standing.

But AI is now at the center of the fight, and that won't end with October.
author: coinbureau
quoted_text:
The internet is going into a LOCKDOWN.

Hundreds of millions of websites are potentially at risk from cyberattacks.

Governments, banks and major platforms have already taken their websites OFFLINE.

Many are already calling it “Black October.”

At the centre of the shutdowns is something most of us have never heard of, but use every day.

PHP, the software behind roughly 7 in 10 websites, has two critical flaws that can let hackers break in without a password.

Dubbed PHP2Shell, both are rated 9.2 out of 10 for severity.

Details began circulating on Oct 20. Emergency fixes arrived the next day, but attackers were already moving.

Cloudflare’s CEO says hacking attempts then jumped from thousands to MILLIONS within hours.

Cybersecurity agencies across several countries are telling PHP site owners the same thing: Patch it now, or take it offline.

Websites have gone dark worldwide, from government portals and hospitals to banks.

CrowdStrike warns these attacks leave almost no trace, so some sites may not know if they’ve been hit.

Around 2.6 MILLION internet-facing servers run PHP, potentially hosting hundreds of sites each.

Over 1.1 million use older versions no longer receiving official PHP updates.

Older installations may need an upgrade to a supported PHP version or a fix from their software provider.

And patching does not remove a backdoor an attacker may already have planted.

Cloudflare also says hackers are now tweaking their attacks to try to slip past its protections.

But PHP isn’t the only security story unfolding.

-Japan’s Onamae suspended ALL Desktop Cloud plans after malware was found on customer servers.

-India’s eMudhra had 8 website-certificate keys so weak, one was literally the number “4”.

-State Bank of India confirmed 3,897 customer records on the dark web.

-Criminals used AI agents to break into 400+ Latin American banks.

-Capcom confirmed a breach exposing 11.7 million email addresses.

-GitLab disclosed a 10/10 severity flaw in versions going back to 2014.

-LiteLLM removed a malware-containing release. Railway reported possible exposure of customer secrets.

None of these has a confirmed link to PHP2Shell.

We’re seeing separate breaches unfold together.

The true number of incidents could take months to come out.

The world is still on alert. Attacks are still coming.

text:
链上美股能预测周一开盘价？|  65分钟Ondo对谈整理

Ondo @OndoFinance 是我目前在 RWA 和链上美股赛道重点关注的项目，同时我也是@OndoPerps的用户，币安广场这场长达一个多小时的专访，@BugsbunnyGG 老师连线了 Ondo 的 DeFi 负责人 Matt，讨论了几个问题：
• 美股半夜和周末休市，遇到突发事件和财报怎么在链上平仓避险；

• 周末美股关门时，链上合约的价格到底是怎么定出来的；

• 怎么用代币化美债（USDY）和苹果现货直接当抵押品开单对冲；

• 微软、谷歌、英伟达大举投入 AI 资本支出，为什么被比作“利润微薄的航空公司”？

嘉宾：大老师Bugsbunny @BugsbunnyGG ｜ Matt Blumberg（Ondo Finance Head of DeFi）@matt_blumberg

我将整场 65 分钟录音整理为纯文字版了👇

1️⃣ 美股永续合约（Perps）vs 传统期权：为什么 7×24 小时交易是刚需

➤ 大老师问：既然市场上已经有传统股票期权了，为什么还要做美股永续合约？

➤ Matt 回答：期权适合持有周期长、对方向有判断但不确定中间走势的人，期权没有强平爆仓风险；但期权要选行权价和固定到期日，每天有时间价值衰减。永续合约没有到期日限制，用户随时可以灵活进出。

➤ 大老师补充：美股大部分股票在盘前盘后无法平仓。现在大量财报发布和大波动都发生在非交易时间，7×24 小时的永续合约让交易者在闭市时多了一个能随时平仓对冲的通道。

2️⃣ 周末休市预言机：周末链上合约价格如何形成

➤ 大老师问：美股周末休市时，Ondo Perps 的价格是怎么确定的？做市商怎么对冲，流动性如何保证？

➤ Matt 回答：周一至周五有交易所公开价格和盘后价格，直接算移动平均；周末休市时，以周五收盘价为基准锚点，根据平台内部交易行为计算移动平均，并设定 10% 或 20% 的硬性波动上限。

➤ Matt 说明：价格偏离周五基准后，通过资金费率机制激励买卖双方付费促使价格回归。算法对齐 TradeXYZ 等做市商标准以保障对冲流动性。内部数据跟踪显示，周末链上交易的价格，通常高度接近周一美股真正开盘时的价格。

3️⃣ 抵押品与对冲：代币化美债（USDY）与股票现货做抵押

➤ 大老师问：用户怎么拿代币化资产做抵押来对冲持仓？有哪些具体场景？

➤ Matt 回答：传统券商放闲置资金没有利息。Ondo 支持拿代币化美债（USDY）当抵押品，在开单交易的同时底层继续享受美债年化收益。

➤ Matt 说明：如果长期持有苹果现货不想卖出（避免卖掉产生资本利得税或卖飞底仓），短期遇到地缘事件想对冲，可以直接把苹果代币当抵押品开出空单，无需变卖现货。

➤ Matt 补充：在其他平台做期现套利，100 美元本金要拆成 50 美元买现货、50 美元开空单，只有 50 美元仓位拿费率；而在 Ondo 可以用 100 美元买现货作抵押开 100 美元空单，全额仓位均可获取资金费率。

4️⃣ 苹果（$AAPL）与其他科技股的策略差异

➤ 大老师分析：苹果放弃了造车项目，在 AI 方面的资本开支很低，自由现金流充沛，管理层风格稳健。持有苹果做抵押，风险低于那些高资本开支的半导体股票。

➤ Matt 回答：波动小、确定性高的资产最适合做抵押品，因此 SPY、QQQ 和苹果这类资产最受欢迎。

➤ Matt 补充：苹果在端侧硬件优势明显，目前很多人购买 Mac mini 或 Mac Pro 在本地运行开源模型，硬件能效比和电费比优秀，还能保护本地隐私。

5️⃣ 科技巨头 AI 高资本支出与“航空业”类比

➤ 大老师分析：一级市场消息显示 Anthropic 的 ARR 预期可能需要打折，实际数据低于卖方预期。微软、谷歌、Meta 资本支出极高，若估值过高，财报季后可能面临股价下修。

➤ Matt 回答：能改变世界的公司不一定等于好股票，这很像航空业。飞机彻底改变了世界，但航空公司利润率普遍很低，因为资本开支极大、燃油成本极高，且各家服务高度同质化。

➤ Matt 补充：当前 OpenAI、Anthropic、DeepSeek 的模型差异不大。像 CoreWeave（$CRWV）这类高资本开支模式依赖资本市场融资，面临对投资回报率的严苛要求；而具有国家防御属性的核心模型若面临资金缺口，政府层面大概率会支持。

6️⃣ 传统企业服务影响与日常实际使用的 AI 工具

➤ 大老师分析：AI 可能会侵蚀埃森哲（$ACN）等传统 IT 咨询公司的初级外包业务，长期会迫使其转型。

➤ Matt 回答：埃森哲这类公司自身也在用 AI 缩减人工成本以维持利润，实际情况比单纯的“被替代”更复杂。

➤ Matt 分享工具：处理核心数据与关键任务更倾向于用 Claude（Anthropic），因其风格偏谨慎稳健；日常做完直播后常使用 Grok 自动提炼核心观点并抓取短视频切片，帮助解决跨时区内容发布的痛点。

Once man has created an intelligence greater than his own, that intelligence should be able to create an intelligence greater than itself, as man whose intelligence is less than its was able to create its intelligence. He was charged with intoxication manslaughter, which carries up to 20 years in prison. A judge revoked his bond twice while the case was pending, and both times he was back out within two weeks.

On Monday he got 10 years of probation, community service, and $535 in fees.

Five boys have lost their father, and the man who killed him just had to pay a small fine and promise not do it again before going back home.

housebets went after stake, shuffle, bc game and duel players

remember when i covered their insane +325% deposit growth? from $4.4m to $18.5m in just 30 days

looks like they managed to steal a shitload of players from competitors, right?

well, we decided to dig deeper and asked @addressableid, a @famcryptospace partner, for some actual onchain data

and damn, the numbers surprised me

in october, on EVM chains:

~14.2k wallets matched the $1 bonus claim pattern
~8.7k had previous deposit history at 4 competing casinos
~1.5k had $10k+ in lifetime deposits

the typical claimant had only ~$500 in previous deposits

and here's something i really didn't expect

out of 23.6k stake wallets with $10k+ lifetime deposits that have been active since july, fewer than 700 claimed. under 3%...

and tbh this looks more like a pilot than a finished strategy. pretty sure they'll keep improving it

so yeah, housebets got everyone's attention, but i wouldn't say they managed to steal stake's whales

also, $18.5m in deposits doesn't mean $18.5m in revenue. we still have no idea how much they actually made

still think the acquisition mechanic is brilliant

now i'd love to see how many of those wallets keep depositing after claiming their bonuses

*EVM-only data, сlaims inferred from $1 deposits, not confirmed user records, tron and solana excluded

author: randhindi
quoted_text:
Text messages with a machine, in and of themselves, are not criminal, immoral, or dangerous, for there is no victim, whatever the content. It is the very same thing as with thoughts—regardless of the content, no thought can be said to create a victim.

• If someone steals info and feeds it into an LLM, it was the theft itself which created the victim, not the subsequent text message.

• If someone uses the output of an LLM to hack a system, it is that subsequent hack which creates the victim, not the text message preceding it.

• If someone threatens harm to themselves or others through messages into a machine, here still the messages themselves cannot be said to have created any victim. 

Imagining otherwise inappropriately reorients blame from its rightful place: the action of harm actually done by a perpetrator.  Thinking harm =/= harm.

As humans integrate AI as an extension of their mind, policing at the message layer means to increasingly police thought itself. 

Which company, which committee, do you trust to police your thoughts? Or do you simply want the thoughts of others policed, and not your own?

author: econoar
quoted_text:
In the case of Lighter:

1. All data is verifiable - you don't have to trust the operator.  Withdraw your funds via escape hatch if Lighter stops operating. There are CLOBs for other products like spot/options where realtime settlement makes a difference, and it is synergistic via portfolio margin

2. Lighter can trivially offer privacy to traders by encrypting data (with the trader's public key) before it's posted to Ethereum. This does not affect the escape hatch. Position level privacy can be mandatory, opt-in, or opt-out. Trades, volume and open interest can remain public, verifiable info while individual trader positions remain hidden

3. No priority fees on Lighter. 

4. Combining onshore/offshore orderbooks is technically possible but that's up to the regulators.

5. Lighter matching engine is centralized and highly performant. There is no tradeoff between speed and security. If there is inefficiency, it is the cost of generating and publishing proofs of correct execution, which is low and continuing to drop quickly.

My goal with @cfosilvia is to build the best piece of software for serious investors who want to control their own money.

The big idea is that AI technology can help these investors navigate the complexities of managing their household finances, especially when it comes to tax, estate planning, investment decisions, and generational wealth transfer. 

Anyone can sign up, connect their financial accounts, and begin talking to Silvia about their finances. The more context you give her, the more helpful she can be. 

My initial suggestion for every user is to connect your accounts and then ask Silvia to interview you, so she gets relevant information that will make her even better at her job. 

Today we have over 20,000 investors and more than $60 billion in assets connected to the platform. The average user is a multi-millionaire and paying users ask Silvia 20+ questions per week. 

Given the product touches personal financial data, it has been important to me since day one that we embrace three core ideas of privacy, security, and accuracy. 

For example, we applied for SOC II certification when there was literally only me and @shaincodes at the company. Almost no one does that, but the privacy and security of our users is front-and-center for us.

Additionally, we have spent the last ~ 6 months rebuilding the AI tech stack to reduce our dependency on frontier models. This has allowed us to improve the accuracy of Silvia's answers on important personal finance topics like tax, mortgage, and credit cards. 

If you search the internet or here on X, you will find tons of people who love the product. They are tired of the amateurish budgeting and saving apps. These individual investors need a product that can help them grow their assets and net worth, not save $5 on Starbucks.

We are proud of the product we have built and think there is tons of room for improvement too. Our team is currently only ~ 10 full-time employees, so we are rapidly shipping new features and products with the hopes of delivering on Silvia's core promise to help serious investors accelerate their net worth growth.

If this approach resonates with you, I would appreciate it if you took a few minutes to sign up for the product and gave it a try. It is free to use when you get started and you only have to pay if you become a power user. 

Try Silvia: https://t.co/bMI7hLeK8s 

Feedback is a gift, so once you have tried the product, please send any ideas on how we could improve it. No idea is too small or too silly. We can only build the best product if we have smart users who share their ideas. 

I appreciate you reading this far and hope you enjoy using Silvia. We are having a blast building it.

author: ErikVoorhees
quoted_text:
Today my office has released a major new report on student enrollment in NYC.

We found that k-12 enrollment in our public schools has fallen by 187k since 2013, with a projected decline of an additional 128k students by 2034.

As total enrollment declines, NYCPS is serving a student population with growing needs. The number of students with disabilities is increasing. In the most recent school year, approximately 73% of students were in poverty and 14% were homeless or living in temporary housing.

Our report finds the drop in enrollment is driven by declining births and families with children leaving NYC, with a particularly notable drop in public-school enrollment as students transition from elementary to middle school.

These trends have massive implications for our schools that we have only barely begin to grapple with. My hope is that this report will spur a long overdue conversation about what the era of falling student enrollment means for NYC, and what we can do to reverse or slow it. 🧵

How the Office of the Texas Attorney General @KenPaxtonTX is violating federal law.

I was kicked out of medical school ostensibly for "professionalism" issues. But I knew this wasn't true. For months, I fought for access to my educational records.

Two months ago, I finally got a glimpse.

Then, last week, under the order of an attorney from the TX AG's office, my access was blocked again -- a violation of federal law.

The Office of the Attorney General under Ken Paxton is helping Texas Tech to violate federal law.

Given how terrible the record is, it's not hard to understand why Texas Tech -- and now the Texas Attorney General -- wants to cover it up and make it go away.

This is what my "professionalism coach" at Texas Tech med school wrote.

Cheryl Erwin, Director of the Center for Ethics, Humanities & Spirituality.

Her notes:

> She compared my case to the Trump indictment.

> She suggested that questioning the unscientific COVID pandemic response -- lockdowns, mask mandates -- was like Trump questioning the 2020 election.

> She said that I "imbibed the cultural atmosphere of conspiracy theories."

> She characterized my position on the pandemic response as believing in a "conspiracy."

> She wrote that my exercising my First Amendment rights was me "making an idiot of himself."

> When I insisted I shouldn't be punished for speaking freely about how the medical profession abused its power, she called me "combative."

To my face, she told me none of these things. She signed off her emails, "Your friend." She promised confidentiality. And just weeks before she gave devastating testimony against me in a rigged hearing, she told me: "I will not abandon you."

She never once talked about what I wrote about on social media to my face. But it's almost all she could write about behind my back.

This is just one part of what's in my records. I got access in January after months of delays. First, one hour to review 2,000 records. Then, after I filed a complaint with the Department of Education, I was able to review them, escorted into a building, university-controlled laptop.

No copies. Even though all records were electronic.

I found things like the above. And so much more.

I filed an amended complaint in federal court using what I'd found in Texas Tech's own records.

Their response?

@KenPaxtonTX's litigation counsel sent me a letter telling me to stop contacting the university requesting FERPA access, that TTUHSC would provide no further access, and that my pending transcript amendment request would be paused indefinitely "until the litigation is resolved."

They said that I have seen the records enough. 1600 documents. Longer than Tolstoy's War and Peace.

They could just send the PDFs. Instead they insist on breaking the law.

They didn't cut off access because I was abusing it. They cut off access because their own records contain their own admissions -- and they would rather shut down a federal statutory right than let me keep viewing.

And here's the thing: what I have seen is only the tip of the iceberg. They have withheld many records. If this is what I have seen, what are they hiding?

I have filed a complaint, and now 5 supplements, with the Department of Education's Student Privacy Policy Office.

I will never, ever quit. Not this year. Not next. Not in 5. Not in 10. Not in 20 years. Not ever.

There will be justice.

@KenPaxtonTX -- Your office is breaking federal law; it is defending an agency that violated the United States constitution; you can withdraw your support any time if that agency's interests diverge with those of the state of Texas; that time is now.

@GregAbbott_TX -- Your university is punishing students for their speech for holding positions you agree with.

@CreightonForTX -- You are the new Texas Tech Chancellor. You are the "conservative". Prove it.

@EDSecMcMahon -- There is no litigation exception to FERPA. I was given 40 hours to review 1,600 documents. Now Texas Tech refuses any further access -- in writing. Your department has my complaint and 5 supplements. Enforce the law.

@EDUnderSecKent -- Texas Tech is breaking federal law, 20 U.S.C. § 1232g(a)(1)(A), 34 C.F.R. § 99.10(b), § 99.32. My complaint has been submitted months ago with supplements. When will the Department of Education do its job?

@TexasTech -- The truth will come out. And everyone will know.

Tomorrow.

The first of the secret recordings, published here. A senior Texas Tech official admitted to me that they didn't believe what they wrote about me in the official documents.

But that it was written in retaliation to my constitutionally protected speech.

His own words. On audio.

text:
Some stream of consciousness commentary on the latest events

Binance hack:

Largest ever crypto hack - from total 6bn, 3bn was frozen (good ratio imo). Binance is plugging the 3bn hole from their own balance sheet and SAFU fund (which is now fully depleted after this)

Its hard to see this event as positive for crypto, the cybersecurity FUD headlines just keep coming. Many people and institutions will now think even harder before entering the space. That being said its remarkable how small the dump was post-hack.

In parallel tech/ AI stocks are dumping as well and BTC is now less volatile than stocks, despite the news. 

I don’t want to sound premature but steady price action in face of big bad news suggests we are bottoming.

The industry wide reaction was quite professional this time, fast communication, USDT and USDC promptly frozen, Aave disabled all the pools to prevent hacker from using them. 

Cautiously optimistic the crypto industry will be hardened through all of these trials by fire and become much more resilient over time.

Otoh its very hard for me to make a case for buying a lot of crypto here, as cybersec is continuing to be an issue across board from exchanges, HW wallets, internet infra etc. 

Gun to head Id actually say its slightly bullish BTC here, just because it does seem its bottomed out, priced in all the FUD remarkably well and it’s the simplest exposure to crypto with smallest attack surface / complexity (sans some quantum/AI breaking cryptography tail event). 

So if any macro situation starts favoring crypto, it should favor BTC first, but it probably pays to wait for midterms to rip the "dems are coming for our coins" bandaid off.

NYSE/ICE + Druck + TradeXYZ/Hyperliquid

ICE and Druckenmiller are working with TradeXYZ to bring Hyperliquid perps to US. The announcement pumped HYPE by 15% (victory lap)

My initial gut reaction is that its bearish other competitors in this arena - e.g. LIT and ZRO - but I slept on it and start to lean bullish for everyone. ICE just fired the first shot but they are not exclusively working with TradeXYZ, they are massive investor in Polymarket, already work with LayerZero's ATLAS etc. etc.

ICE competitors and other institutions heard the shot and will now enter the arms race even faster (feeling FOMO / fear of being disrupted) and will try to bring their own guns to the fight. 

Some of them will perhaps also tap Hyperliquid, but its reasonable to assume some will want to differentiate and compete with different partners.

So in general bullish HYPE (and better yet PURR going above 1 mNAV same to CYPH on ZEC run), and bullish the whole "perps + tokenisation with US institutions" basket - LIT, ZRO, BP etc

However we should recalibrate this view after the midterms dust settles. Depending on how exactly they end and what the political rhetorics will be after.

We could see anything from mild impact (dems will ignore crypto to focus on AI, or they will silently support it seeing the adoption as inevitable) 

to severe (crypto will be a poster child of Trump&Co shenannigans that mustn't go unpunished)

Its fair to think many institutions are waiting for this signal

text: 省流：别听毒攻略吹牛逼，企图用老iPhone代替硬件钱包。
author: GuHype
quoted_text:
Over the past two weeks iPhones have been publicly jailbroken more than once, and most people treated it as a bit of tech drama and scrolled on. I want to use it to talk about something that matters more to people in crypto: wiping an old iPhone, putting it in airplane mode and using it only to hold your seed phrase is not as safe as most people think. If it's an iPhone 11 or older, the problem lives in the chip, and no iOS update will fix it.

Quick recap of what happened. On October 16 at Hexacon in Paris, the Calif team jailbroke an iPhone 18 Pro running iOS 27.0.1 live on stage. The jailbreak survived a reboot, they had root, and they got past MIE, the hardware memory protection Apple added starting with the A19 specifically to stop spyware. In the same session they showed attacks that get in through a single click in Signal or iMessage. A week later, on the day iPhone Duo went on sale, they jailbroke that too. Apple shipped iOS 27.2 on October 26, and Calif says most of the bugs they used are now fixed. Then on October 30, Ikotas Labs, the Japanese team that just won Pwn2Own, posted that they had jailbroken 27.2 as well. Their video only shows swapped icons and the version number, though, so I'm treating it as unconfirmed for now.

For most people on a recent phone who keep it updated, none of this is a reason to panic. Before chains like these get patched, they usually sit with spyware vendors and forensics companies, and the odds of an ordinary person being specifically targeted are low. Update to 27.2 and you've done what you need to.

The people I actually want to warn are those using an old iPhone as a cold wallet. iPhone 4S through iPhone X have checkm8 in the BootROM, made public in 2019. This June, usbliter8 went public, covering the iPhone XS, XR, the 11 series and the 2nd-gen SE. The BootROM is boot code burned into the chip at the factory. Apple can't patch it with a software update, so these devices will carry the hole for as long as they exist. Exploiting it doesn't need a network either. Once someone has your phone in hand, they put it into DFU mode and plug in a custom USB board (the public research used a $5 Raspberry Pi Pico 2), and they can run their own code before iOS even boots. Airplane mode makes no difference here.

I don't want to overstate it. On models like the XS and 11, the BootROM bug alone won't hand over your seed phrase, because your passcode and the Secure Enclave are still in the way. The trouble is that these remaining layers are exactly where people tend to cut corners: a 6-digit passcode, an iOS version years out of date with a pile of public n-days, a short wallet app password. On some older models, forensic tools use bugs like this to brute-force the passcode. And if your wallet app encrypts the seed with nothing but a short password, once that encrypted file is copied off, the attacker can take it home and keep guessing offline, with no attempt limit. Old iOS versions also have a charging port problem. ChoiceJacking, published in 2025, lets a malicious charger pose as a keyboard and approve the data-access prompt for you. Apple only closed that in iOS 18.4.

One more thing about this kind of attack: when you get your phone back, nothing looks off. In security circles it's called an evil maid attack. A hotel room, a security check, lending your phone to someone to charge — any time it's out of your hands for a while, there's an opening. A lot of people only find out their phone was touched after their assets are already gone.

My advice:

1. Check which iPhone holds your seed phrase (Settings → General → About). If it's an iPhone 11 or older, move to a newer model before storing a seed on it.

2. If you've already stored one there, no need to panic. When you get a chance, generate a brand-new seed phrase in an environment you trust and move your assets over. It has to be a whole new seed. A fresh address under the old seed won't help.

3. If your phone has ever been out of your hands for a while, say held for inspection at a border, don't wait. Migrate as in step 2 as soon as you can.

4. Update your daily iPhone to iOS 27.2 (Settings → General → Software Update). If you haven't moved to 27 yet, install at least 26.7.2.

5. Switch to a long alphanumeric passcode (Settings → Face ID & Passcode → Change Passcode → Passcode Options). A 6-digit PIN has only a million possible combinations. Make your wallet app password longer too.

6. Carry your own charger. Don't use public USB ports, random power banks or cables you don't know.

7. If you hold a lot or are likely to be targeted, consider turning on Lockdown Mode (Settings → Privacy & Security → Lockdown Mode). It blocks wired connections while the phone is locked.

8. Any "iOS 27 jailbreak download," or any tutorial asking you to install a certificate or configuration profile, is a scam or malware. Neither Calif nor Ikotas has released any tools.

If you like using an iPhone as a cold wallet, go with a newer model and keep it on the latest iOS. There's no public BootROM exploit for the iPhone 12 or later, and if something does turn up, Apple can still fix it with an update. With really old devices, the risk sits in the chip itself, and updating iOS won't get you around it.

text:
In the case of Lighter:

1. All data is verifiable - you don't have to trust the operator.  Withdraw your funds via escape hatch if Lighter stops operating. There are CLOBs for other products like spot/options where realtime settlement makes a difference, and it is synergistic via portfolio margin

2. Lighter can trivially offer privacy to traders by encrypting data (with the trader's public key) before it's posted to Ethereum. This does not affect the escape hatch. Position level privacy can be mandatory, opt-in, or opt-out. Trades, volume and open interest can remain public, verifiable info while individual trader positions remain hidden

3. No priority fees on Lighter. 

4. Combining onshore/offshore orderbooks is technically possible but that's up to the regulators.

5. Lighter matching engine is centralized and highly performant. There is no tradeoff between speed and security. If there is inefficiency, it is the cost of generating and publishing proofs of correct execution, which is low and continuing to drop quickly.

Further to my post about @NYSE working to bring @HyperliquidX onshore, major credit to @ChairmanSelig and the Trump administration for making all of this experimentation possible. 

There’s only one way of finding out if something is useful to the marketplace and I’m excited for us to find out. I do have some questions:

1. What is the benefit of trading perps on-chain on a regulated exchange? Isn’t the main benefit of trading on-chain to operate in a trustless (aka non-kyc’d) environment in order to minimize friction, and/or to be able to enter into atomic transactions in order to receive what you are buying in realtime? Since a perp is not an asset, that obviously isn’t helpful. 

2. @standuquesne - are you aware that if you trade on Hyperliquid, the world will be able to track your positions and trades in real time? Do you see that as a benefit?

3. Hyperliquid has priority fees - a mechanism that enables market participants to pay to see information first, or even prioritize orders in front of the queue. Is this consistent with CFTC core principles?

4. Will it be possible to combine the liquidity of the offshore order-book with the onshore order-book?

5. If not, wouldn’t it be better to list perps in a traditional (centralized) order-book on a regulated exchange and not have the inefficiencies that on-chain matching introduces?
