Anatomy of a Stablecoin:
Stablecoins are some of the most complex products in the crypto neobank space.

What sits behind a digital dollar is hard to follow. The reserves, the banks, the mint, the chains. The legal side is even harder: who can issue it, which rules apply, what changes from coin to coin. That's true whether you're building your own stablecoin or just deciding which one to use.

I built Anatomy of a Stablecoin to simplify it:
https://t.co/LY64LHPwVi

It lets you explode a stablecoin and see everything that happens in between. You can flip it, zoom in and follow $100 in and out.

Here's everything inside:

Learn: 12 questions, in the order people actually ask:
1. What is a stablecoin?
2. What is inside it?
3. What backs every token?
4. Where is the money actually held?
5. How are tokens created and destroyed?
6. Who checks your identity before a coin is made: KYC, AML and sanctions screening
7. What the token actually is: a smart contract that tracks balances and can mint, burn and freeze
8. How does money get in and out?
9. What keeps the price at  $1?
10. What makes it legal in the US?
11. Who builds each piece?
12. How do real stablecoins compare?

The 7 layers of a stablecoin:
1. Compliance: KYC, AML monitoring, sanctions screening and the Travel Rule
2. Reserves: cash, T-bills under 93 days, overnight repos and government money funds
3. Custody: segregated accounts, and holders get first claim if the issuer fails
4. Mint and burn: a token is created when a dollar comes in and destroyed when it goes out
5. Smart contract: ERC-20, SPL, TRC-20, plus the freeze, pause and blocklist functions
6. Blockchains: Ethereum, Solana, Base, Tron, BNB Chain, the XRP Ledger, Polygon, Arbitrum, Stellar, TON, Avalanche and Citrea
7. The token: the balance you actually see in your app

Follow the money:
• Money in: Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal, Venmo, Cash App, bank transfer and crypto
• Money out: bank payouts, push to card, P2P apps, card spend and crypto
• Watch $100 go through every step: fund, verify, reserve, mint, deliver, trade, redeem, pay out

16 real stablecoins:
1. XO Cash: Exodus's dollar, issued by MoonPay on M0, on Solana
2. ctUSD: the dollar for Bitcoin apps on Citrea, issued by MoonPay on M0
3. USDT: the biggest, about $182B, issued from El Salvador
4. USDC: Circle's coin, about $71B, the largest US regulated stablecoin
5. USDe: Ethena's synthetic dollar, backed mostly by stablecoins it lends out plus hedged bitcoin and ether
6. DAI: no company issues it; smart contracts create it and SKY holders govern it
7. USD1: World Liberty Financial's dollar, issued by BitGo, a federally chartered trust bank
8. USDG: Paxos's Global Dollar, where partners can get up to all of the reserve income
9. PYUSD: PayPal's dollar, issued by Paxos
10. RLUSD: Ripple's dollar, issued by a New York trust company Ripple owns
11. USDD: TRON's dollar, backed mostly by TRX
12. U: an offshore coin on BNB Chain that says it has no license
13. TUSD: one of the oldest, with most of its reserves caught up in a court fight
14. EURC: Circle's euro coin, about 60% of the euro stablecoin market
15. SoFiUSD: issued directly by a US national bank
16. Phantom CASH: issued by Bridge on Solana
For each one: issuer, license, reserves, reports, chains, supply, who can mint directly and whether holders earn yield
• Check the supply yourself: links to CoinMarketCap, DefiLlama and each issuer's reserve report
• Race up to 4 dollar coins side by side and watch the same $100 move through each one

Who builds it:
• MoonPay, Circle, Tether, Paxos, Anchorage, Bridge, M0, Ethena and Coinbase, plus the analytics, custody and liquidity players
• Click a company and the model lights up the layers it runs
• See which coins each one really issues. 

4 approaches to launching a dollar token:
1. Become the issuer: Obtain the required authorizations and take responsibility for reserves, redemption and compliance. Most direct control; generally the heaviest operational burden.
2. Use an issuance partner: Providers such as MoonPay, Paxos, Anchorage, or Bridge offer branded stablecoin issuance. You manage the brand and customer experience; the issuer's responsibilities and regulatory permissions depend on the specific arrangement.
3. Build on shared infrastructure or an existing stablecoin: Use a platform like M0, potentially with an issuance partner. PYUSDx is an example: MoonPay issues PYUSDx against PYUSD at 1:1; Paxos issues the underlying PYUSD. This adds another issuer and redemption layer.
4. Create a synthetic dollar: Use collateral plus derivatives hedges to target a dollar value, as Ethena does with USDe. This is a different backing model. Ethena's staking product, sUSDe, accrues rewards; simply holding USDe does not.

The rules:
• The 8 GENIUS Act requirements, checked live as you change the design: licensed issuer, 1:1 eligible reserves, segregated reserves, monthly reports, redemption at $1, an AML program, sanctions and freeze controls, no yield to holders
• The 4 issuer routes: bank subsidiary, federal nonbank, state issuer under $10B, and offshore
• Drag the price off $1 and see how fast it comes back. Strong reserves snap back, weak ones don't
• Switch to an algorithmic coin and watch it break the way TerraUSD did in 2022

Build your own
• Pick how you issue (a platform like M0 or PYUSDx, a partner, or your own license), plus the reserves, controls, chains and how money gets in and out
• Score it against GENIUS in real time, out of 8
• Get a launch plan with a timeline: about 12 weeks on a platform, about 20 with an issuing partner

Two modes
1. Simple: one circle that shows where your money goes when you add money, spend with a card or withdraw
2. Pro: every layer, every rail, every rule

149 sources behind it, all linked on the page:
https://t.co/sSyJcetlHz

Spot something wrong, or have an idea to make it better? DM me here or on LinkedIn. All feedback helps.

One shotted this with Claude Opus 5.5.

Turns out building a crypto neobank is easy. Everyone can do it today.

How to build a neobank in 3 easy steps:

1. Choose your region: the US, Europe, Latin America or Asia

2. Choose your stablecoin: USDC, USDT, or USDC plus cash at the bank

3. Of course I didn't one shot this and spent way too much on tokens 🤣. And no, you can't build a neobank in 3 easy steps.

It's extremely hard, and it's quickly becoming a commodity. If you think you can build one because you know how to set up a wallet with Privy, you're in for a surprise.

Every choice changes what happens under the hood: the tech stack, the region, the goal, the stablecoin. Each one comes with its own rules and tradeoffs. Margins are thin. The moat is distribution.

So I built Programmable Money so you could brainstorm and actually understand how crypto neobanks work.

Hit Explode and the app comes apart in 3D, like an X ray. You see every layer hiding behind the screen. How money gets in and out, the stablecoin under your balance, the wallet and the chains it runs on, earn and borrow, tokenized assets and the card.

Click any piece and it tells you what it does, who runs it and which rules apply. Then press Play and follow $100 as it moves through the whole thing, step by step.

It's the easiest way I've found to dissect the tech and actually understand it.

3. Latin America
4. Asia

This article is a good step toward understanding how things really work. However, quite a few factors related to the experimental setup need to be taken into account if you want to draw more reliable conclusions:

1. The optimal shape of each architecture may differ under compute-optimal settings.
2. The optimal initialization of each parameter may differ across architectures.
3. Different architectures may respond quite differently to different optimizers.
4. Differences in training stability and the health of “internal metrics” can lead to drastically different results, even for the same architecture.
5. Architectures may respond differently to varying degrees of overtraining (tpp).
6. Different architectures may respond quite differently to different data distributions (i.e., different learning objectives).
7. The difficulty of scaling up can vary considerably across architectures.

There are many more nuances that need to be carefully addressed to obtain consistent results.

In the case of Lighter:

1. All data is verifiable - you don't have to trust the operator.  Withdraw your funds via escape hatch if Lighter stops operating. There are CLOBs for other products like spot/options where realtime settlement makes a difference, and it is synergistic via portfolio margin

2. Lighter can trivially offer privacy to traders by encrypting data (with the trader's public key) before it's posted to Ethereum. This does not affect the escape hatch. Position level privacy can be mandatory, opt-in, or opt-out. Trades, volume and open interest can remain public, verifiable info while individual trader positions remain hidden

3. No priority fees on Lighter. 

4. Combining onshore/offshore orderbooks is technically possible but that's up to the regulators.

5. Lighter matching engine is centralized and highly performant. There is no tradeoff between speed and security. If there is inefficiency, it is the cost of generating and publishing proofs of correct execution, which is low and continuing to drop quickly.

text:
The cobra effect is one of the more interesting phenomena in startups. Once you see it, you start noticing it everywhere, in your team, your metrics and now your AI agents.

It's basically when you reward people for hitting a number, and they find a way to hit it that makes the real problem worse.

The name "Cobra Effect" comes from a story about Delhi under British rule. There were too many cobras in the city, so the government offered a reward for every dead cobra people brought in. 

Instead of hunting them, people started breeding cobras so they could kill them and collect the money!

When the government found out and ended the program, the breeders let their snakes go, and Delhi ended up with more cobras than before!

I'm noticing that AI agents are making this more common. Basically, an agent will chase whatever number you give it, all day, without asking why. Tell it to make the tests pass and it might rewrite the tests. Tell it to close support tickets faster and it might close them without solving anything. It happens.

The best startups have already figured out the fix with people. Airbnb tracks bookings and host cancellations together. HubSpot takes back sales commission when a customer churns early.

The video breaks down how they did it, and it's the same playbook you'll want for your agents.

NEW ROBOTICS STARTUP: China now has its OpenAI for robotics!

Archon Robotics is a Shanghai embodied-AI startup building what it calls a Whole-Body Intelligence framework, a generalist humanoid foundation model assembled from three pieces:
1. pretraining on large-scale human whole-body motion data to establish interaction priors
2. a context-aware behavioral foundation model aimed at "precise, stable loco-manipulation with terrain interaction"
3. an efficient post-training on real-robot data to turn those priors into deployable skills.

Its stated ambition is to be the OpenAI for Humanoid Robotics in China!

The founding team comes out of end-to-end autonomous driving: Hongyang Li is Founder and CRO, an assistant professor at HKU, who led UniAD and holds a 2026 RSS Early Career Spotlight; Tianyu Li is co-founder and CEO, previously a core architect of Huawei's ADS 4.0; Li Chen is co-founder and Head of AI and was UniAD's first author.

The company has raised a seed round of hundreds of millions of yuan from ZhenFund, Gaorong Capital, IDG Capital, 5Y Capital, Gobi Partners, a Gobi and HKU joint fund, MiraclePlus and the Shanghai Zhiyuan Academy.

Also worth mentioning: the team is behind the CVPR 2023's Best Paper for arguing that perception, prediction and planning should be one differentiable stack optimized for the driving objective rather than a chain of hand-specified modules.

Their framing of Whole-Body Intelligence, one foundation model that moves, perceives, reasons and acts, is the same argument with a different embodiment, which is the opposite bet made by many research approaches lately.

"There is this term called the crack spread... It's not a net margin that anybody is actually making... But it is useful because if you look at any given refinery, just like you might look at any given model, you want to ask this basic question which is, 'Is this making any money?'"

text:
Text messages with a machine, in and of themselves, are not criminal, immoral, or dangerous, for there is no victim, whatever the content. It is the very same thing as with thoughts—regardless of the content, no thought can be said to create a victim.

• If someone steals info and feeds it into an LLM, it was the theft itself which created the victim, not the subsequent text message.

• If someone uses the output of an LLM to hack a system, it is that subsequent hack which creates the victim, not the text message preceding it.

• If someone threatens harm to themselves or others through messages into a machine, here still the messages themselves cannot be said to have created any victim. 

Imagining otherwise inappropriately reorients blame from its rightful place: the action of harm actually done by a perpetrator.  Thinking harm =/= harm.

As humans integrate AI as an extension of their mind, policing at the message layer means to increasingly police thought itself. 

Which company, which committee, do you trust to police your thoughts? Or do you simply want the thoughts of others policed, and not your own?

Since we began using self-assessment in June, it has surfaced misuse that our other safeguards weren’t designed to catch. 

Because Claude has already read the conversation, self-assessment is very efficient. And unlike classifiers, which target a discrete set of harms, it draws on Claude’s own judgment, so it gets more accurate as our models improve.

Beam  (@b1m_ai) #SN105 is positioning itself as the “programmable bandwidth” layer for enterprises and AI agents: rather than forcing organizations to replatform, it lets them move, stream and exchange data across cloud storage, enterprise applications and distributed infrastructure. Its focus is making large scale data movement something an agent can initiate, monitor, and complete as part of an automated workflow.

Why It Matters

Beam’s core idea is simple: data should move wherever it is needed: between S3, Cloudflare R2, S3-compatible stores, Hugging Face, and other systems without manual infrastructure work or vendor lock-in. The network supports bidirectional movement across AWS, GCP, Azure and private infrastructure, making it especially relevant for enterprises with data spread across multiple environments.

For AI agents, this becomes a native capability. Beam’s Hermes & OpenClaw integrations lets agents estimate, start, track and manage transfers, while Beam Rooms provide end-to-end encrypted communication and data exchange between agents, applications and connected systems.

Enterprise-scale Performance

Beam has also demonstrated that the approach can handle serious workloads: it moved 1TB in 2m 43s, coordinating hundreds of concurrent streams across independent operators on its decentralized bandwidth network. That is a strong proof point for enterprise-scale datasets and agent-driven pipelines.

The Bigger Picture

Beam is building an open, distributed network to move data between storage, applications and AI compute effectively turning bandwidth into programmable infrastructure. For enterprises, that could mean faster migrations, analytics, backups and model training data pipelines; for agents, it means the ability to orchestrate data movement autonomously rather than treating it as a separate IT task.

In short: Beam is trying to make enterprise data movement as easy and as automatable as calling an API, while proving it can move terabyte sized workloads in minutes.

text:
Bill Ackman just sat down with Nicolai Tangen for 53 minutes.

The man famous for fighting CEOs now gets thank-you notes from them. And he owns the exact stock Chris Hohn just dumped.

My favorite takes:

1. A great company is one you could buy today, have the stock market close for 20 years, and still sleep fine. If he can't model it 10 to 20 years out, he doesn't look.

2. He thinks only 200 to 300 truly great businesses exist on earth. Pershing Square owns 12 to 14 of them. 48 employees. 9 investment professionals.

3. Won't touch anything driven by commodity prices, interest rates or regulators. "Extrinsic factors we can't control."

4. Favorite structure: the royalty collector. A business that throws off cash it never has to reinvest.

5. A quality company that missed earnings used to fall 3 to 4%. Now it can fall 30 to 40%. Index funds shrink the float. Leveraged short-term money does the rest. That gap is his entire opportunity set.

6. He bought Amazon after the tariff crash. Meta and Microsoft after the market punished them for raising capex. Those three are now roughly a third of the fund. Hohn cut Microsoft from 10% to 1%. Same chair, opposite trade.

7. On AI: it shortened everyone's horizon. A 10-K gets read in seconds and capital chases the next quarter. Every business he owns is either AI, should be AI, or gets disrupted by it.

8. When AI makes intelligence cheap, creativity is what's left. He doubts any model could have produced Einstein's relativity from everything written before it.

9. His real edge is permanent capital. Most money in asset management can leave daily, quarterly or annually. "You can't be dispassionate if your clients are just going to pull your money."

10. In 1969 Buffett ran a $100M hedge fund taking 25% of profits above 6%. He gave it up for a $100,000 salary and a textile mill. He traded the best fee deal in finance for money that couldn't leave.

11. Ackman's textile mill is Howard Hughes. Pull capital out of real estate. Put it into a specialty insurer. Invest the float like Buffett. Target: 80% insurance within a decade. He hired a team built for a $50 to 100B insurer to run one with under $2B of capital.

12. The Icahn story. 1998. Ackman sells him a real estate stake with "schmuck insurance": flip it within 3 years at a profit, split the gain. Icahn flips it. Owes $ 4.5M. Refuses. Ackman sues and wins. Icahn appeals on day 179 of every 180-day window, all the way to the Supreme Court. Years later Icahn takes the other side of Ackman's Herbalife short. Pershing loses about $ 1B.

13. His conviction test: find the best short-seller on your position and try to rebut every argument. He applies the same rule to opinions outside markets.

14. His main information source is X. Follows about 1,000 accounts. Thinks it runs 1 to 2 weeks ahead of traditional media. He has pitched Musk on a button that shows the best counter-argument under every post.

15. The honest footnote. Since 2004 his strategy compounded 15.6% a year vs 11.0% for the S&P 500. Since his listed fund launched at the end of 2012: 12.5% vs 15.2%. Even a great record depends on where you start counting.

16. His daughter suffered a brain hemorrhage this year. He is now building a brain recovery institute in New York and believes the blind will see again within years, not decades.

17. Tangen asks: advice to young people? Ackman passes on Buffett's version. Show up on time. Answer people who reach out. Do the right thing when nobody is watching. You can't decide to become Michael Jordan. You can decide to have character tomorrow.

The headline: two of the best quality investors alive sat in the same chair this year and read Microsoft in opposite directions.

Hohn sold Microsoft because AI might break the moat. Ackman bought Microsoft because the market panicked over what the moat costs to defend.

author: BillAckman
quoted_text:
Leftist mainstream media outlets piled on this week to express outrage at my observation, during a speech in Grand Rapids for Mike Rogers, about the troubling dearth of scientific output from the world’s 22 Arab nations over the past five decades. These reporters — @fatimathefatima @AP, @Kanishka183 @Reuters, @rachel_roubein @washingtonpost, @baylisswagner @nytimes, @stevebenen @MSNOWNews — omitted critical context, presumably to bestow plausibility on their accusations that my statements were racist and Islamophobic.

However, my speech was not a critique of Arabs or Islam, but of Islamism (also known as “Islamofascism” or “Political Islam”), a toxic ideology conceived and promoted by the terrorist group, the Muslim Brotherhood. Let’s see which reporters take the time to read this post and then correct their stories.

Criticizing Islamism is neither Islamophobic nor racist. Islamism is a violent corruption of mainstream Islam that summons adherents back to the seventh-century ideal of bloody jihad, the homicidal and suicidal religious zealotry that propelled a motley cadre of desert nomads to conquer half the world. Sheikh Ahmed El-Tayeb, the Grand Imam of Al-Azhar — the Muslim equivalent of the Vatican and the highest authority in Sunni Islamic thought — has rejected Islamism as “false Islam” and a “perversion of the Islamic religion” and accused it of “barbaric crimes.”

Islamism is intensely anti-American, anti-Western, and hostile to modernity. It is explicitly contemptuous of democracy, constitutional government, capitalism, minority rights, gay rights, women’s rights, free speech, and virtually all personal freedoms. Its central aspiration is for a global caliphate ruled by a single theocratic despot with absolute power to impose sharia law that dictates every aspect of human conduct. The Muslim Brotherhood’s founder, Hassan al-Banna, taught that the highest aspiration for a Muslim was martyrdom in the achievement of that goal; the purpose of every Islamic nation is to “perfect the industry of death” until world domination is accomplished.

I pointed out in my speech that the Muslim Brotherhood’s antipathy for modernity is a dramatic departure from Islam’s historical affinity for science and learning. During the Muslim Golden Age, spanning the eighth through the fifteenth centuries, Muslim leaders dignified Islam’s wealth and power by promoting a brilliant flowering of innovation and scholarship in science, mathematics, philosophy, art, literature, astronomy, pharmacology, psychology, engineering, architecture, medicine, and navigation that continues to enrich the world today. Arab leaders fostered an intellectual ferment unmatched by any other in human history. A long line of enlightened caliphs assembled—and abundantly rewarded—an unparalleled galaxy of jurists, scientists, physicians, philosophers, musicians, artists, poets, and wits. Muslim rulers elevated the role of reason and tolerance, cultivating a milieu of religious and intellectual freedom—where Jews and Christians also flourished—and encouraged sages of various faiths and ethnicities to collaborate and freely exchange ideas.

For five centuries, Arabic was the world’s most learned and literary tongue and the lingua franca of science and scholarship. Most mosques had libraries (Córdoba hosted 600!). Muslim princes in the tenth century often had more books in their personal collections than existed in all of Europe. Baghdad had 100 bookstores in AD 891. England would have to wait another 420 years until 1309 to see paper for the first time.

Islam’s second Golden Age during the Ottoman Empire (1299–1922) birthed a cosmopolitan and pluralistic civilization centered in Constantinople that yielded additional bonanzas in poetry, music, art, and a tsunami of scientific innovation from coffee to water pumps, steam engines, gears, surgical scalpels and clamps, the first smallpox vaccine, and the cannons that allowed the Ottomans to dominate Europe to the gates of Vienna.

In 1928, six years after the Ottoman Empire collapsed, the Muslim Brotherhood began to spread its dark strain of violent fundamentalism from Egypt to Palestine and across the Muslim world. Islamism’s contagious proliferation ended the dialogue between Islam and the intellectual classes and demoted the role of reason in Islamic life. The Muslim Brotherhood’s principal philosopher, Sayyid Qutb, was contemptuous toward public education in science, math, and philosophy, believing that the only source of truth is the Koran. For Qutb, the purpose of education was not to celebrate life, or to nourish the intellect, but to indoctrinate children in the art of war, the glorification of death, and a blind obedience to an autocratic caliph.

Qutb railed against reason, which he considered the seed of apostasy. He sought to silence the humanities and viewed science as a sinister displacement of religion. He derided pluralism, rationalism, innovation, and tolerance. In doing so, he deprived Islam of its modern potential and its own greatest inheritance: the confidence to learn from the world, preserve its wisdom, and surpass it.

In his obituary for Muslim culture, The Closing of the Muslim Mind (2010), Robert R. Reilly recognizes that Qutb’s outlook dooms his followers to inertia. A religion that values obedience over initiative, that seeks to obviate independent reason, is a religion of violence. Where there is no framework for rational mediation, all disputes must be settled by force.

It didn’t worry Qutb that discouraging education in physics, mathematics, medicine, or engineering would atrophy intellectual and economic development in the Muslim world. Qutb explained that Muslim countries were so far behind the West in the sciences and technology that there was no hope to catch up. Muslims, he preached, should do what they do best—study the Koran and embrace martyrdom as the path for achieving global dominion: “The Muslim community today is neither capable of nor required to present before mankind great genius in material inventions, which would make the world bow its head before its supremacy.”

Qutb’s diatribe against Muslims competing in science and technology was nothing less than civilizational malpractice—especially given that he wrote it in 1964. Had Japan, Singapore, or South Korea accepted Qutb’s logic in 1964, they would have opted out of modernity. Instead, they chose to accept the challenge of competition. Their decision to engage has yielded stunning achievements that transformed their nations into economic and technological superpowers and enriched all of humanity.

The anti-intellectualism of Islamism—the rejection of evidence and the scientific method, the hostility toward objectivity, the suppression of contrary information, the deification of dogma, the embrace of pseudoscience, the contempt for reason as the path for discerning objective truth, and Islamism’s association of science with immorality—has helped close off the Islamic mind. The staggering metrics of intellectual and scholastic enfeeblement in Muslim nations attest to Islamism’s systematic squandering of human capital including the creative potential among the world’s two billion Muslims.

Korea issued 260,000 patents in 2024, while nine Arab countries, including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, issued fewer than 10,000 in total, with 8,000 of these coming from a single nation—Saudi Arabia—which has made herculean efforts in recent years to de-Islamize its society. Japan, which represents about 1.5% of the world’s population and is practically devoid of natural resources, granted 306,855 patents in 2024 alone. There are 127 million Japanese, compared to 500 million Arabs.

According to Hillel Ofek’s 2011 analysis, there were a mere nine scientists, engineers, and technicians per thousand citizens in Islamic nations. The global average was forty-one. Among the 1,800 universities in Muslim nations, only 312 housed scholars who had published articles in journals.

Muslims represent 26% of the world’s population, and Muslim countries control half the world’s crude oil resources and 40% of natural gas resources. And yet the 53 Muslim countries combined publish only 5% of the world’s scientific literature. Hillel Ofek points to a 1989 study showing that in a single year, the United States published 10,481 frequently cited scientific papers, but during that same year, Arab countries published just four. A 2002 analysis of Arab science in Nature magazine identified only three scientific areas of excellence from Islamic countries: desalination, falconry, and camel reproduction. According to Nobel laureate physicist Steven Weinberg in 2011, “for forty years I have not seen a single paper by a physicist or astronomer working in a Muslim country that was worth reading.”

Contrast the Arabs’ dismal record of intellectual achievement in modern times with that of their closest cousins, the Jews, nearly all of whom live in democratic societies with laws that separate religion and politics.

Keep in mind that Jews, who number 15.8 million worldwide, represent a mere 0.2% of the world population. As of 2025, no Muslim has ever received the Nobel Prize in medicine or economics, and only four Muslim scientists—all living in Western democracies—have received the Nobel Prize in chemistry or physics. In contrast, some 200 Jews have received Nobel Prizes in science. About 26% of Nobel Prizes in math and science, 28% in medicine, 40% in economics, and 39% in chemistry have gone to Jews. Since 1901, some 22% of Nobel Prizes in all categories have gone to Jews.

Genocidal hatred against ALL Jews and Christians and other minorities is foundational to Islamism. Only in the West does Jew hatred pretend to require the alibi of Palestine or hide behind anti-Zionism. Muslim Brotherhood cosmology describes the universe as a cosmic, existential war between Islam and Jews that began with Muhammad and which only one side can survive. “Since Islam subdued them [in Medina],” Qutb warned, “they are unforgiving and fight furiously through conspiracies, intrigues, and also through proxies [the United States] who act in the darkness against all what Islam incorporates.” Islamist utopia will only emerge when every Jew is exterminated. Jews in Qutb’s theology are not just political adversaries, but perpetual and metaphysical evil. “The Jews,” he said, “are behind materialism, animal sexuality, the destruction of family, and the desolation of society.”

And Jewish genocide, for Islamism, is more than a theoretical aspiration. In 1948, the world’s 22 Arab nations were host to 750,000 Jews living in communities that predated Muhammad by 1,000 years. Today, there are virtually no Jews in those nations: Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Libya, Algeria, Yemen, Mauritania, Somalia, Sudan, Jordan, Gaza, or the PA-governed areas of the West Bank; in Nazi terminology, they are Judenrein: Jew-free. There are fewer than 1,000 Jews in Tunisia, down from 105,000. In 1948, Christian populations represented 20% of those nations; today they represent 4%. These are the real ongoing genocides of the Mideast.

Adolf Hitler’s Nazi regime bonded with early Islamists over their shared Jew hatred. The Nazis became the principal funder of the Muslim Brotherhood in the 1930s, and the Muslim Brotherhood operated propaganda, espionage, and sabotage operations for the Nazis during World War II. Joseph Goebbels and an army of Nazi and ex-Nazi propagandists built the Muslim Brotherhood’s powerful propaganda machine in the 1930s, ’40s, and ’50s. The massive influx of money from Iran and the Gulf States starting in the 1990s turned this operation into an amplifier of unmatched power that makes Goebbels look like a piker. A global propaganda barrage by this outfit has distracted Hamas’s Western dupes from Islamism’s authentic genocides by persuading them that Israel committed a genocide in Gaza, even though, according to the CIA Factbook, Gaza’s population has actually increased since October 7, 2023.

Islamism is genocidal against Christians and Jews, but among its most pitiful victims are the Arab societies that suffer the misfortune of living under its rule. Despite all their petroleum wealth, Muslim countries have slipped behind Asia and Latin America in virtually every metric of political freedom, technological progress, and social well-being. Islamism’s merger of politics and religion has robbed Islam of its intellectual vigor and doomed most Muslim populations to living in stifling tyrannies with little freedom to elucidate their thoughts and speech or fulfill their creative potential. Those countries are predictably stagnant, unable to evolve in the modern world. The dark shadow of fundamentalism over scholarship and progress has proven toxic to the Muslims’ transition to modernity. The very civilization that practiced tolerance and celebrated pluralism and dialogue, filled a thousand libraries with its books, gave the world observatories and universities, and stunning innovations in science, has become closed, aggrieved, and violent, and averse to reason, curiosity, freedom of inquiry, and scholarship.

All 22 Arab nations in the Mideast and North Africa are autocratic dictatorships. Almost all are apartheid states that legally restrict the rights of minorities. Gays in many of the nations are put to death. Under sharia law, women have little more rights than cattle. They live stunted lives behind veiled faces, enduring systematic servitude, legalized domestic violence, child marriage, chattel slavery, and public stoning for adultery, which is legal for their husbands. In September 2021, the Taliban made it illegal for girls to attend school after age 12. The Taliban’s Vice and Virtue law forbids women from speaking aloud in public.

If you want to understand the Muslim Brotherhood’s vision for society, look no further than Gaza. Hamas, which rules Gaza, is the Palestine branch of the Muslim Brotherhood. Palestinians have received over 4X per capita in international aid than Europeans received under the Marshall Plan. (See Clawson 2002.) Europe used its money to rebuild 17 nations. Palestinians couldn’t build themselves even one. Under Hamas’s iron fist, Gaza squandered its share on bombs, weapons, extravagant salaries for its billionaire kingpins, and a billion-dollar bunker and tunnel system built for its warriors—but off-limits to its citizens. Gaza remains a stunted and stagnant, impoverished society under tyrannical oppression, with no free speech or other basic freedoms. Hamas governs through force, including brutal crackdowns on discourse, public executions of dissenters and collaborators, tight controls on humanitarian aid distribution, and onerous taxes on almost every activity. No elections have occurred since Hamas took over in 2007. Instead of building a nation, Hamas has transformed Gaza into a death cult wallowing in victimhood, nursing aggrievements, addicted to violence, resentments, and yearning for a seventh-century miasma. Hamas nurses Palestinian infants from birth on genocidal hatred of ALL Jews—not just Zionists—and indoctrinates children in the savagery and unspeakable barbarism that the world witnessed on October 7. Hamas shows its contempt for the Palestinian people by deploying them as child soldiers and civilian shields, and placing rocket launchers and ammo dumps in schools and hospitals. Hamas’s greatest strengths are its propaganda operation and its willingness to impose unlimited pain on its own population to achieve its ideological goals.

Islamist governments like Iran, Hamas, and Hezbollah distract their populations from their misery by blaming the myriad social ills and the predictable government failures on scapegoats: Jews, Zionists, and America. They’ll have us believe that all their derelictions are the result of the evil Zionists, the “Little Satan” Israel, and the “Great Satan,” the U.S. And just as victimhood is paralyzing to personal growth, it deprives Islamist nations of national success by robbing its practitioners of agency. Islamism’s cult of victimhood and its coterminous abolition of self-criticism have stagnated global Islam and locked it in hatred, violence, brooding resentment, and isolationism. Referring to the Arab world, Fouad Ajami described this as “a political tradition of belligerent self-pity.”

Contrast Gaza’s failures with the successes of its closest neighbor, Israel, a tiny sliver of swamp and desert 1/600th the size of its Arab neighbors, that blossomed into an agricultural juggernaut and a global economic and technological superpower. Jews took one of the few places in the Mideast with no oil, gas, or other resources, and despite being surrounded by enemies, they nevertheless turned the barren landscape into a vibrant, pluralistic democracy where Jews and Arabs vote as they please; worship according to their convictions; serve beside each other in the judiciary, the army, and political leadership; and enjoy equal rights. Women and gays in Israel have all the rights of men, and Israel’s biggest annual celebration is the Pride parade in Tel Aviv. As the only democracy in the Mideast, Israel is a robust and heroic outpost for freedom and Western values.

And Israel is merely a nugget among the bounties bestowed by Jews on Western civilization. There is no ethnic or religious group that has contributed more than Jews to the welfare of humanity or to the advancement of liberal democracy. Jewish traditions of ethics and thinking have shaped Western civilization and global progress through foundational moral concepts, including our monotheistic Christian belief system with its roots in Judaism, milestone scientific breakthroughs, medical innovation, and innumerable cultural achievements in art, literature, education, health, and entertainment. Relative to their proportion of the population, the astonishing contributions by Jews have been breathtaking. An abbreviated list would include medical advances like the polio vaccine (Jonas Salk, Albert Sabin), chemotherapy and immunology (Paul Ehrlich), streptomycin and the age of antibiotics (Selman Waksman), penicillin (Ernest Chain), pacemakers (Paul Zoll), and blood typing (Karl Landsteiner).

In sciences, a short list of Jewish luminaries would include Albert Einstein (theory of relativity), Niels Bohr (quantum mechanics), and Paul Berg (first recombinant DNA molecule).

Jewish contributions to business and technology include Google (Sergey Brin), Meta (Mark Zuckerberg), Oracle (Larry Ellison), Salesforce (Marc Benioff), Intel (Andrew Grove), and Dell Technologies (Michael Dell).

Jews virtually created the American entertainment industry, including founding six of the eight major Hollywood studios responsible for 75% of the classic Golden Age movies. They also revolutionized laughter. A 1978 TIME magazine survey found that 80% of professional comedians were Jewish.

The major figures of twentieth-century Western thought—Jesus Christ, Sigmund Freud, Albert Einstein, and Karl Marx—were all Jewish. Twenty percent of philanthropic giving in the United States comes from Jews. Jews compose twenty-five percent of America’s most generous givers. They are overrepresented on lists of secular organizations that benefit human rights, social security, higher education, personal freedom, and constitutional rights. They represent 14% of doctors and 29% of psychiatrists. quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

author: Alchemy
quoted_text:
Binance’s update is a useful case study in what incident readiness requires once funds are already moving.

A compromised endpoint reached the withdrawal path. No private keys leaked, yet ~$6.3B left across more than ten chains in ~20 min.

Freezes started in less than 1 hour after funds first left Binance. Ability to respond fast depended on three things that had to already exist: fresh on-chain data, relationships with issuers and blockchain teams that can trace and freeze funds, and the operational authority to pause the service and revoke access.

The educational takeaway for infrastructure teams is that the speed of the freeze is downstream of the quality of the preparation. Detection alone is not enough if the escalation path, the data, and the permission to act are still being negotiated while the drain is underway.

Silver Lining: crypto industry worked together quickly to cauterize the attack!

author: ErickAGIx
quoted_text:
New challenge on Yukon: Circuit Breaker https://t.co/vpuIh2CnbR

It took 38 years to raise the best proven circuit lower bound from 3n to 3.1n. Days before this launch, an AI model pushed it to 3.5n.

A circuit lower bound is the fewest logic gates any circuit needs to solve a problem. Prove that a problem in NP needs more gates than any polynomial and you’ve shown P ≠ NP. That would settle whether every problem that’s easy to check is also easy to solve, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.

We’re still far from that bound. Circuit Breaker, built with UCLA Math+AI, is where the push continues.

“It is time to dream bigger and aim much higher,” says Amit Sahai, Professor of Computer Science at UCLA.

text:
Reddit just showed what AI is doing to the internet.

It lost over $7 BILLION in a day after warning Google's AI is cutting its traffic.

Its stock closed down 29.2% on Friday, its worst day ever, and is now down 41% in eight straight sessions.

The reason came out on its earnings call.

CEO Steve Huffman said Google's bots are still reading Reddit's pages as much as ever.

But instead of sending people to Reddit, Google's AI Mode now answers their questions directly.

He said AI Mode doesn't drive traffic to Reddit, or to anyone else as far as he knows.

Reddit lost over 1 MILLION visits a week from search in October.

It now warns its daily users could fall by a low double digit percentage this quarter if the decline continues.

And it isn't just Reddit.

Chegg has lost over 99% of its value since 2021.

Stack Overflow's monthly questions fell from over 200,000 at their peak to just 3,862 last December.

For over 25 years, Google was how people found the rest of the internet, and that era may now be ending.

author: bitcoin2themars
quoted_text:
莫信观察｜UP 最早成交价到开盘一小时约 2,610 倍，90% 买单进了 25 天蓄水池

@tapeupio 的 UP 在 10/31 22:32 开盘。最早一笔即时成交的平均价格约 0.000004859 BEM，23:38 页面价是 0.01268431 BEM，前后约 2,610 倍。

这个数字只能描述最早一笔已经成交的 UP，不能当成第一批买家整张订单的收益。UP 这次开盘用的是 10% 即时买入、90% 进入 Bid Reservoir，剩下的 BEM 要在 25 天里继续买。

🐋 100 BEM 是怎么进场的

按交易页现在的参数，下单 100 BEM：

- 约 10 BEM 当场买成 UP，成交价跟着当时的盘面走
- 约 90 BEM 进入 Bid Reservoir，在后面 25 天分批执行
- 卖出没有 25 天分期，持有人可以直接卖
- 每笔另收 1% BEM 手续费；1.5% UP 建设税单独进入奖励池，两项不能相加成 2.5% 协议收入

我 10/21 拆经济模型时写的是官方文章里的 30% / 70% 示例。PoB 的即时比例本来可以配置，这次 UP 实际开盘页用的是 10% / 90%。

这意味着现在下单，只有一成资金拿到了当下价格。后面九成会按未来 25 天的价格继续成交，最终拿到多少 UP、整张订单的平均成本是多少，现在还算不出来。

🐋 2,610 倍怎么来的

TapeUP 最早一条成交记录：

- Total：50.01311662 BEM
- Amount：10,291,884.01398906 UP
- 对应平均价格约 0.000004859 BEM/UP

23:38 页面价是 0.01268431 BEM/UP，两者相除约 2,610 倍。页面同时显示 +254,958.8%，它用的是平台自己的参考起始价，所以和最早完整成交均价不完全一样。

如果成交表的 Total 只记录即时成交部分，按 10% 比例倒推，这一笔对应的原始买单规模约 500 BEM，另有约 450 BEM 进入蓄水池。交易页没有把这个表格口径写清，这组倒推需要项目方确认；它没有计推荐加速和手续费。

🐋 开盘第一秒发生了什么

22:32:59 的 8 笔即时成交：

- 合计成交 104.292 BEM
- 合计买到 13,936,194.98 UP
- 占 2,100 万总量的 66.36%

如果同一口径成立，首秒原始买单规模约 1,043 BEM，约 939 BEM 进入后续 25 天的蓄水池。最早一笔的 Amount 占总量 49.01%，这是初始成交量，不代表这个地址现在还持有这么多。

🐋 蓄水池比流动性还大

23:38 页面快照：

- Bid Reservoir：13,643.87 BEM，约 27.45 万美元
- 流动性：7,298.91 BEM，约 14.69 万美元
- 市值：约 536 万美元
- 24h 成交量：约 13.24 万美元

蓄水池是当前流动性的 1.87 倍。如果简单平均摊到 25 天，约等于每天 545.8 BEM、1.10 万美元的待执行买盘；实际每天多少，要看订单进入时间、后续新增买单和加速规则。

这批 BEM 会形成持续买盘，也会成为持币人的退出对手盘。买单被拆成 25 天，卖单却能当场执行；只要卖压大过当天释放的买盘，价格一样会跌。

🐋 这个价格还在 TapeUP 内部

UP 现在是 TapeUP Universal Ledger 里的 Token ID 1，还不是普通钱包能直接持有的 ERC-20。页面的跨链门槛是 1,000 万美元，23:38 完成 53.6%。

现在的 536 万美元市值，是页面价乘 2,100 万总量；流动性只有约 14.69 万美元，市值是流动性的 36.5 倍。这个报价能说明盘面走到哪，不能说明有 536 万美元可以按当前价格退出。

所以“开盘涨了 2,610 倍”更准确的写法是：最早一笔即时成交均价到 23:38 页面价约 2,610 倍。整张买单最终赚了多少，要等剩余 90% 的 BEM 在 25 天里执行完才知道。

quoted_text:
Further to my post about @NYSE working to bring @HyperliquidX onshore, major credit to @ChairmanSelig and the Trump administration for making all of this experimentation possible. 

There’s only one way of finding out if something is useful to the marketplace and I’m excited for us to find out. I do have some questions:

1. What is the benefit of trading perps on-chain on a regulated exchange? Isn’t the main benefit of trading on-chain to operate in a trustless (aka non-kyc’d) environment in order to minimize friction, and/or to be able to enter into atomic transactions in order to receive what you are buying in realtime? Since a perp is not an asset, that obviously isn’t helpful. 

2. @standuquesne - are you aware that if you trade on Hyperliquid, the world will be able to track your positions and trades in real time? Do you see that as a benefit?

3. Hyperliquid has priority fees - a mechanism that enables market participants to pay to see information first, or even prioritize orders in front of the queue. Is this consistent with CFTC core principles?

4. Will it be possible to combine the liquidity of the offshore order-book with the onshore order-book?

5. If not, wouldn’t it be better to list perps in a traditional (centralized) order-book on a regulated exchange and not have the inefficiencies that on-chain matching introduces?

text:
Agent 写代码已经不稀奇了，真正麻烦的是跑了半小时突然报错，前面的工作全白干。

微软开源的 Agent Framework 已经超过 1.4 万 Star，重点就是解决 Agent 在实际生产环境中的可靠性问题。

几个核心功能：

-多 Agent 编排：支持串行、并行、任务交接和群组协作
-断点恢复：通过 Checkpoint 保存状态，支持恢复执行
-人工审批：关键操作暂停，确认后继续
-可观测性：集成 OpenTelemetry，追踪执行过程和错误
-多模型支持：兼容 OpenAI、Azure OpenAI 等服务

支持 Python 和 .NET，MIT 开源。

现在 Agent 最大的问题不只是能不能完成任务，而是失败后能不能恢复、出了问题能不能定位。

你用 Agent 开发时，最头疼的是它做错事，还是做到一半突然卡住？

https://t.co/HEYPlocgCY

text:
英伟达创始人黄仁勋在专访里，点破了一个绝大多数人全搞反的 AI 用法。

他说他从来不信任何一个 AI 给出的现成答案，他的核心心法，是把同一个问题扔给几个不同的大模型，让它们在后台互相挑刺批评。

很多人的默认习惯极其糟糕脆弱，
输入一个问题，屏幕吐出一大段看似逻辑严密的文本，看一眼就直接照单全收。

把单一大模型的单次回答当成绝对真理，结果模型稍微产生一点幻觉，自己就顺着错误的逻辑一路掉进坑里。

老黄在视频里公开的这套操作，直接把工具降维成了一场辩论赛。

他拿到一个答案，第一句话永远先反问：你确定这是你能给出的最佳答案吗？

接着他会把这个 AI 吐出来的结论，原封不动喂给另一个模型，让它们在后台互相审查、公开互撕。

这就像去医院看大病，没人会只听一个大夫的一面之词，你一定会找三位医生交叉问诊。

他每天干的，就是把同一个问题抛给不同模型，逼着它们把各自的逻辑死穴全给扒出来，最后由他自己坐在裁判席上，把所有结论里最硬核的部分提炼出来。

提问从来不是为了偷懒省事，而是逼着你先完成最深度的推演。

质疑答案、组织多个模型相互对质，本质上是在用高强度的批判性思维，给自己的肉身大脑做抗阻训练。

把 AI 当答案机器的人，脑子会越来越钝，变成算法的复读机，

把 AI 当辩论对手的人，借着几个模型对抗的火花，正在把自己的判断力打磨成冷酷的终审法官。

顶级玩家的核心壁垒，
从来不是得到了什么现成答案，而是他拥有把所有答案放在聚光灯下反复拷打的质疑力。
author: AYi_AInotes
quoted_text:
X 新任产品负责人 Peter Sellis 不愧是当世最顶级的产品经理，他一句话就把硅谷最顶级的战略心法挑明了：看懂 SpaceX 为什么敢主动淘汰最赚钱的猎鹰 9 号，你就会明白为什么绝大多数公司的规划全是在慢性自杀。

Peter其实给我们掏出了一套极其残酷的产品逻辑：绝大多数平庸公司死于被对手干掉，而顶级公司全部死于不敢对自己开枪。

很多团队做业务规划，本质上是在做自欺欺人的线性推演。

看今年赚了多少钱，看手头有什么资源，然后小心翼翼地在现有的地盘上修修补补，生怕动了既得利益者的蛋糕。

这种顺推思维做出来的东西，往往就是更便宜的旧时代残次品。

但 Sellis 讲的倒推法，直接把时间轴倒了过来。

它绝不是从今天去猜明天，而是强行逼自己站在未来的终局往回看：
如果未来十年后人机交互的标配是轻量化智能眼镜，那我们今天就算把手机屏幕做烂也毫无意义，现在每一行代码都必须全部为那个终局服务。

最狠的是他把这套方法，直接对标到了 SpaceX 当年那个近乎自杀的疯狂决定上。

猎鹰 9 号明明是全人类商业航天史上最赚钱、发射成功率最高的王牌火箭，现金流好到可以躺着吃二十年；

但马斯克反手就要把它彻底淘汰，把全部身家性命押注在连炸了几次的 Starship 星舰上。

这就像当年科尔特斯率军登陆后亲手烧掉退路的战船一样，不给自己留一丝苟活的余地。

Sellis 感叹说，全世界几乎没有哪家大公司能做到 SpaceX 这种程度。

因为人性骨子里都在恋战舒适区，宁愿在一条注定沉没的大船上数钞票，也不愿意跳进冰水里去造下一艘核潜艇。

其实这里有一个极度冷酷的反直觉真相：
商业世界最危险的状态，从来不是你面临绝境，而是你手里正捧着一只利润丰厚的金饭碗。

敢亲手砸碎自己最赚钱的现金牛，
往往是在未来大浪打过来时，唯一能保住整条命的活路。

text:
你的利润，也是你的本金。

很多老韭菜都有一个坏习惯：因为入场早、成本低，就觉得回撤没什么，大不了再扛一轮牛熊。

但市场可不会因为你的成本低，就少收你一分钱。

交易中有个非常反直觉的认知：

大多数人习惯盯着K线的最低点，计算自己赚了多少；真正需要警惕的，却是从最高点下来，你已经回撤了多少。

举个例子：

你用100万赚到了200万，随后回撤50%，账户又回到100万。

从成本看，你没亏钱。

从净值最高点看，你已经亏掉了100万。

更残酷的是，回撤和回本在数学上并不对称。

回撤10%，需要上涨11.1%回本。
回撤20%，需要上涨25%回本。
回撤30%，需要上涨42.9%回本。
回撤50%，需要上涨100%回本。
回撤80%，需要上涨400%回本。

公式很简单：

回本所需涨幅 = 回撤幅度 ÷ (1 - 回撤幅度)

回撤越深，回本难度就越呈非线性增长。

这也是为什么我认为，交易员应该给自己设定一条纪律：

以损定仓，尽量把账户最大回撤控制在20%以内。

这背后其实还有凯利公式的逻辑。

凯利公式追求的是长期资本的几何增长率，而复利最怕的就是大幅回撤。

假设一笔交易有60%的胜率，盈亏比1:1。

凯利公式给出的理论最优下注比例是20%。

但这不代表每笔交易都应该拿20%的账户资金去冒险。

因为满凯利虽然在理想模型下最大化长期对数收益，却也意味着更剧烈的净值波动。

如果采用半凯利，把单次风险预算降到10%，理论增长速度会有所牺牲，但回撤风险也会明显降低。

更重要的是，现实交易中的胜率和赔率都是估计值，市场也从来不会严格按照你的数学模型运行。

凯利告诉你理论上能冒多大风险，最大回撤纪律决定你实际上愿意承受多大风险。

假设账户100万，单笔止损距离为5%。

如果只允许单笔亏损账户的1%，那么：

允许亏损 = 100万 × 1% = 1万

最大名义仓位 = 1万 ÷ 5% = 20万

这就是以损定仓。

先确定自己最多能亏多少，再反推应该买多少，而不是先决定买多少，再祈祷市场别跌。

当然，单笔1%的风险预算并不意味着账户最大回撤一定不会超过20%。连续亏损、跳空、滑点和相关性风险都可能让实际损失超出预期。

交易的终极目标，从来不是证明自己能扛住多大的回撤，而是让自己的资本始终保有下一次下注的能力。

利润一旦进入账户净值，就应该享有和原始本金同等的风险保护。

浮盈不是已经落袋的利润，但回撤掉的浮盈，是实实在在消失的财富。

市场不会记得你的成本价。

真正决定你复利终点的，是净值曲线，而不是持仓成本。

text:
> Why does the worst rise to the top in a society rife with broken politics? 

“When the plan fails—and it always fails—coercion is needed. You need people willing to do what honest people refuse to do. The system doesn't promote the best; it selects those with no scruples. And to rally a majority around the plan, nothing works better than a common enemy: the rich, the foreigner, the dissenter.”
author: garrytan
quoted_text:
Je parle souvent de La Route de la servitude de Friedrich Hayek. Je vais être direct : pour moi, quiconque lit ce livre en étant sain d'esprit et n'en ressort pas libéral et profondément anti-étatiste est soit fou, soit stupide, soit corrompu. Soit les trois à la fois.

Voici pourquoi. Masterclass.

D'abord, l'homme.

Friedrich Hayek naît à Vienne en 1899, dans un empire qui se croit éternel. À 18 ans, il est sur le front italien. Quand il rentre, l'empire n'existe plus. Il voit l'Autriche sombrer dans l'hyperinflation, les économies d'une vie effacées en quelques mois.

Il devient l'élève de Ludwig von Mises, celui qui avait démontré qu'un planificateur sans prix libres navigue à l'aveugle. En 1931, il part enseigner à Londres et devient le grand rival intellectuel de Keynes. En 1938, il voit son pays natal avalé par Hitler sous les acclamations de la foule. Il prend la nationalité britannique.

C'est là, en pleine guerre, entre 1940 et 1943, qu'il écrit son livre. Pas contre les nazis : tout le monde l'était déjà. Contre quelque chose de bien plus dérangeant. Il voit les élites anglaises, les meilleurs esprits, les gens les mieux intentionnés, reprendre exactement les idées qui avaient mené l'Allemagne au désastre. Planification, direction de l'économie, organisation « scientifique » de la société.

Il dédie le livre « aux socialistes de tous les partis ». Tout est dit.

Trois éditeurs américains le refusent. Il sort en 1944, s'épuise en quelques semaines, puis le Reader's Digest le condense pour des millions de lecteurs. Keynes lui-même, son grand adversaire, lui écrit qu'il en approuve moralement et philosophiquement presque chaque ligne. Trente ans plus tard, Hayek reçoit le prix Nobel. Thatcher relit le livre en 1974 et change la trajectoire de l'Angleterre.

Le titre, d'ailleurs, est un hommage à un Français : Tocqueville, qui avait vu venir le despotisme doux.

Maintenant, ce que dit le livre. En clair.

Première idée : personne ne sait assez pour planifier.
La connaissance qui fait tourner une économie n'est dans aucun bureau. Elle est éparpillée dans des millions de têtes : l'agriculteur qui sait quand sa terre est prête, le commerçant qui sent son quartier changer, l'artisan qui connaît son fournisseur. Le prix libre est le seul système capable de rassembler tout ça en un signal. Remplacez les prix par un plan, et vous remplacez le savoir de millions de gens par l'ignorance de quelques-uns.
Deuxième idée : contrôler l'économie, c'est contrôler la vie.
On croit que l'économie est un domaine à part, matériel, secondaire. Faux. Celui qui contrôle les moyens contrôle les fins. S'il décide de ce que vous pouvez produire, acheter, chauffer, cultiver, il décide de la façon dont vous vivez. Il n'y a pas de liberté politique sans liberté économique.

Troisième idée : une démocratie ne peut pas se mettre d'accord sur un plan.
Tout le monde veut « un plan ». Personne ne veut le même. Le Parlement débat, tergiverse, se divise. L'impatience monte, et on finit par dire : laissons faire les experts. On délègue à des agences, des commissions, des autorités « indépendantes ». La démocratie ne meurt pas d'un coup d'État. Elle se dessaisit elle-même, par lassitude.
Quatrième idée : l'État de droit contre l'arbitraire.
Dans un pays libre, l'État fixe des règles générales, connues à l'avance, les mêmes pour tous, comme le code de la route. Vous savez à quoi vous attendre et vous construisez votre vie autour. Dans un pays planifié, l'État décide au cas par cas : qui a droit à quoi, quel secteur survit, quelle région est sacrifiée. Ce n'est plus la loi qui gouverne, c'est la volonté de quelqu'un.

Cinquième idée, la plus terrible : pourquoi les pires arrivent au sommet.
C'est le chapitre que tout le monde devrait lire. Quand le plan échoue, et il échoue toujours, il faut contraindre. Il faut des gens prêts à faire ce que les gens honnêtes refusent de faire. Le système ne promeut pas les meilleurs, il sélectionne ceux qui n'ont pas de scrupules. Et pour souder une majorité autour du plan, rien ne marche mieux qu'un ennemi commun : le riche, l'étranger, le récalcitrant.
Sixième idée : la fin de la vérité.
Un plan a besoin que tout le monde y croie. Alors l'information devient un instrument. Ce qui sert le plan est vrai, ce qui le gêne devient de la « désinformation ». La propagande n'est pas un accident du dirigisme. C'est une nécessité.

Et la leçon centrale, celle qui glace le sang : ceux qui ouvrent la route ne sont pas des monstres. Ce sont des gens sincères, cultivés, bien intentionnés. Ils veulent la justice, la sécurité, le progrès. Ils ne voient pas où mène le chemin. Les monstres arrivent après, quand le terrain est prêt.
Ce livre est une bouteille à la mer. Hayek nous a laissé le mode d'emploi pour reconnaître la pente avant qu'elle devienne un précipice.

Et que fait l'Europe ? Elle rejoue le livre, chapitre par chapitre.
Les règles générales remplacées par des milliers de normes au cas par cas. Des décisions qui pèsent sur nos vies prises par une Commission que personne n'a élue et que personne ne peut renvoyer. Des plans à vingt-cinq ans pour l'énergie, l'agriculture, l'industrie, l'automobile, comme si quelqu'un à Bruxelles savait mieux que 450 millions d'Européens ce qu'il faudra produire en 2050. Et quand ça échoue, on ne remet jamais le plan en cause. On ajoute une couche : une taxe, une interdiction, un régulateur.

Le plus cruel, c'est l'ironie. En 1939, Hayek défendait l'idée d'une fédération européenne. Mais une fédération où ni le centre ni les États ne pourraient diriger l'économie. Une union pour libérer les échanges, pas pour piloter les vies. Nos européistes ont gardé le mot « fédération » et jeté tout le reste. Ils ont construit exactement ce contre quoi il nous mettait en garde.
Ils avaient le livre à portée de main. Ils refont les mêmes erreurs, avec les mêmes bonnes intentions et le même mépris pour ceux qui doutent.

Je ne crois pas que l'histoire se répète à l'identique. Je crois qu'elle rime. Au XXe siècle, la route de la servitude a mené au pire : des tyrans fous, des peuples broyés, des dizaines de millions de morts. Ceux qui avaient ouvert la route n'avaient jamais voulu ça.

J'espère que, pour une fois dans l'histoire, nous saurons nous arrêter avant. Que nous n'attendrons pas le tyran pour comprendre où menait le chemin.

Hayek nous a tout dit il y a quatre-vingts ans. La seule question est de savoir si nous saurons le lire à temps.

Lisez La Route de la servitude. Puis offrez-le à quelqu'un que vous aimez.

quoted_text:
Ten million people have watched a comedian accidentally destroy the entire TED talk industry.

He filmed the talk once at TEDxNewYork in 2014 and openly admitted he had nothing to say.

Speaking coaches charge $5,000 to teach the exact tricks he used in 6 minutes to say nothing at all.

His name is Will Stephen. He is a comedian from Late Night with Seth Meyers who was invited to give a real TED talk and used it to prove the format is a costume anyone can wear.

Every TED speaker opens with a question, tells a personal story, cites a scientist, and shows a chart. Stephen did all four in six minutes with zero content.

His entire formula fits on a napkin.

Gesture with both hands. Ask the audience a question anyone can answer. Tell a mildly embarrassing story so they say aww. Point to a stranger on a slide and call them important. Flash a chart of random numbers. Wear glasses with no lenses. The audience will think you are brilliant.

That last trick alone has probably cost the public speaking coaching industry a hundred million dollars in sessions clients should have skipped.

"If you watched me on YouTube with the sound off, you would think I was a genius."

That is Will Stephen on the TED stage, three minutes into the talk he was paid to give. He wasn't lying.

Executives pay $15,000 for a keynote coach and still open with a joke the room never laughs at. Founders rehearse their pitch for weeks and still sound like Stephen at minute four, saying "wagga wah, gabba gabba" with authority.

The talk is free on YouTube. The method is written across every TED speaker's playbook for ten years.

Stephen still writes for Seth Meyers. Almost none of the ten million viewers have stopped nodding at empty slides since.

The formula is free. The willingness to actually say something before your next keynote, pitch, or townhall is the entire edge.

quoted_text:
Anatomy of a Stablecoin:
Stablecoins are some of the most complex products in the crypto neobank space.

What sits behind a digital dollar is hard to follow. The reserves, the banks, the mint, the chains. The legal side is even harder: who can issue it, which rules apply, what changes from coin to coin. That's true whether you're building your own stablecoin or just deciding which one to use.

I built Anatomy of a Stablecoin to simplify it:
https://t.co/LY64LHPwVi

It lets you explode a stablecoin and see everything that happens in between. You can flip it, zoom in and follow $100 in and out.

Here's everything inside:

Learn: 12 questions, in the order people actually ask:
1. What is a stablecoin?
2. What is inside it?
3. What backs every token?
4. Where is the money actually held?
5. How are tokens created and destroyed?
6. Who checks your identity before a coin is made: KYC, AML and sanctions screening
7. What the token actually is: a smart contract that tracks balances and can mint, burn and freeze
8. How does money get in and out?
9. What keeps the price at  $1?
10. What makes it legal in the US?
11. Who builds each piece?
12. How do real stablecoins compare?

The 7 layers of a stablecoin:
1. Compliance: KYC, AML monitoring, sanctions screening and the Travel Rule
2. Reserves: cash, T-bills under 93 days, overnight repos and government money funds
3. Custody: segregated accounts, and holders get first claim if the issuer fails
4. Mint and burn: a token is created when a dollar comes in and destroyed when it goes out
5. Smart contract: ERC-20, SPL, TRC-20, plus the freeze, pause and blocklist functions
6. Blockchains: Ethereum, Solana, Base, Tron, BNB Chain, the XRP Ledger, Polygon, Arbitrum, Stellar, TON, Avalanche and Citrea
7. The token: the balance you actually see in your app

Follow the money:
• Money in: Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal, Venmo, Cash App, bank transfer and crypto
• Money out: bank payouts, push to card, P2P apps, card spend and crypto
• Watch $100 go through every step: fund, verify, reserve, mint, deliver, trade, redeem, pay out

16 real stablecoins:
1. XO Cash: Exodus's dollar, issued by MoonPay on M0, on Solana
2. ctUSD: the dollar for Bitcoin apps on Citrea, issued by MoonPay on M0
3. USDT: the biggest, about $182B, issued from El Salvador
4. USDC: Circle's coin, about $71B, the largest US regulated stablecoin
5. USDe: Ethena's synthetic dollar, backed mostly by stablecoins it lends out plus hedged bitcoin and ether
6. DAI: no company issues it; smart contracts create it and SKY holders govern it
7. USD1: World Liberty Financial's dollar, issued by BitGo, a federally chartered trust bank
8. USDG: Paxos's Global Dollar, where partners can get up to all of the reserve income
9. PYUSD: PayPal's dollar, issued by Paxos
10. RLUSD: Ripple's dollar, issued by a New York trust company Ripple owns
11. USDD: TRON's dollar, backed mostly by TRX
12. U: an offshore coin on BNB Chain that says it has no license
13. TUSD: one of the oldest, with most of its reserves caught up in a court fight
14. EURC: Circle's euro coin, about 60% of the euro stablecoin market
15. SoFiUSD: issued directly by a US national bank
16. Phantom CASH: issued by Bridge on Solana
For each one: issuer, license, reserves, reports, chains, supply, who can mint directly and whether holders earn yield
• Check the supply yourself: links to CoinMarketCap, DefiLlama and each issuer's reserve report
• Race up to 4 dollar coins side by side and watch the same $100 move through each one

Who builds it:
• MoonPay, Circle, Tether, Paxos, Anchorage, Bridge, M0, Ethena and Coinbase, plus the analytics, custody and liquidity players
• Click a company and the model lights up the layers it runs
• See which coins each one really issues. 

4 approaches to launching a dollar token:
1. Become the issuer: Obtain the required authorizations and take responsibility for reserves, redemption and compliance. Most direct control; generally the heaviest operational burden.
2. Use an issuance partner: Providers such as MoonPay, Paxos, Anchorage, or Bridge offer branded stablecoin issuance. You manage the brand and customer experience; the issuer's responsibilities and regulatory permissions depend on the specific arrangement.
3. Build on shared infrastructure or an existing stablecoin: Use a platform like M0, potentially with an issuance partner. PYUSDx is an example: MoonPay issues PYUSDx against PYUSD at 1:1; Paxos issues the underlying PYUSD. This adds another issuer and redemption layer.
4. Create a synthetic dollar: Use collateral plus derivatives hedges to target a dollar value, as Ethena does with USDe. This is a different backing model. Ethena's staking product, sUSDe, accrues rewards; simply holding USDe does not.

The rules:
• The 8 GENIUS Act requirements, checked live as you change the design: licensed issuer, 1:1 eligible reserves, segregated reserves, monthly reports, redemption at $1, an AML program, sanctions and freeze controls, no yield to holders
• The 4 issuer routes: bank subsidiary, federal nonbank, state issuer under $10B, and offshore
• Drag the price off $1 and see how fast it comes back. Strong reserves snap back, weak ones don't
• Switch to an algorithmic coin and watch it break the way TerraUSD did in 2022

Build your own
• Pick how you issue (a platform like M0 or PYUSDx, a partner, or your own license), plus the reserves, controls, chains and how money gets in and out
• Score it against GENIUS in real time, out of 8
• Get a launch plan with a timeline: about 12 weeks on a platform, about 20 with an issuing partner

Two modes
1. Simple: one circle that shows where your money goes when you add money, spend with a card or withdraw
2. Pro: every layer, every rail, every rule

https://t.co/sSyJcetlHz

quoted_text:
@treetowntree and i created neuron lens: a database of every single neuron and attention head in qwen 3 8b and gemma 4 12b read using the R-lens (a J-lens variant) and what we call the "S-lens". you can find it at https://t.co/DI2Cpajc3M, along with the tools we used to make it. 

using the R-lens to read neurons' input and output projections turns out to be very effective at determining what a neuron does. we're able to legibly read what a majority of neurons do when fired: the lens qualitatively predicts the result of steering over 90% of the time!

the same trick lets us read attention heads' QK circuits and OV circuits, showing us both what they attend to and what they do with it. however, the R-lens has two important flaws: its accuracy degrades in early layers, and it can't separate the MLP block and the attention block.

we found ways around both these issues. we first modified the r-lens by fitting it on input tokens rather than output tokens to get the s-lens, which is accurate in early layers but inaccurate in late layers. we then fitted R- and S-lenses to the activations after attention but before the MLP to get "mid-lenses", which are much better at deciphering MLP inputs and attention outputs. using both of these techniques, we were able to interpret most of the models' layers.

Gemini Agent is built for high-ceiling work where EACH task gets its own computer.  

You can choose Gemini 4 Argon or Claude Opus 5.5. 

10 things that make it a universal work Agent (read till the end to see what a REAL work agent looks like): 

1. One Agent, one API
Chat, autonomous objectives, and code generation from a single interface. Assign it work, schedule it, or have it respond to events.

2. Coworker agents with their own identities
It creates job-specific sub-agents, each with its own identity, and computer running in parallel for hours or days.

Each Coworker agent gets its own Workspace account: an agent email, calendar, Drive, and presence in your company directory. You mention it in Chat. It acts under its own identity, not yours, and sees only what you share.

3. Everywhere, including headless
Web, iOS, Android, Windows, Mac, command line, Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack. It also runs as a headless agent with no dedicated interface.

4. Work 24/7 in the cloud
It keeps one set of memories, context, and personalization graph across every device and channel. Work that takes hours or days keeps running after you close your laptop. You never have to re-brief it.

5. Layers of memory that improve over time
- Session: the task in front of it, even when it runs for days.
- Semantic: a structured knowledge base it builds as it reads documents, talks to people, and works with other agents.
- Procedural: how a job gets done, including skills it writes for itself.
- Episodic: everything it has done before.

6. Proactive by design
It does not wait to be prompted. An email asking you for a deck gets flagged as delegatable, one click to hand off. Your inbox ranks by what matters, not by what just arrived, and tells you why.

7. Tools and skills, with company registries
Salesforce, ServiceNow, Jira, Git, Confluence, Microsoft 365, Slack, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, your desktop files, and any MCP server inside or outside your network. Teams publish their own tools and skills to a shared company registry.

8. Model Choice so you are not locked in
It runs each job on the model that fits best, running  across the Gemini and Claude models from Anthropic today, with other private and open models to come. 

9. Governed like an employee
Every agent gets a cryptographically attested identity with least-privilege permissions, and an audit trail attributed to the agent rather than a person. Agents run in a sandbox behind Agent Gateway, an AI network firewall. Write the policy once and it applies to every agent.

10. Costs you can actually cap
Smart Routing puts each workload on the model with the best performance at the lowest cost. Set a hard spend limit in Cloud Billing and that project's agent pauses until you resume it in one click.

Thank you for reading so far. Stay tuned for updates. 

We are 100% committed to make it the best Agent for work.

text:
I just love that this resurfaced on my timeline. I'm 90% with Jeff.
A lot of people hunt for system hacks and believe humans can only do a few hours of focused, quality work a day, and that anything beyond that has diminishing returns. It's hard, but your nervous system can adapt to long hours of grinding. And enough grinding naturally teaches you to work smart.

That doesn't mean smart work doesn't matter. It means you shouldn't be hyper-fixated on it. Get the work done first, as well as you can. Getting smarter at it is a byproduct of consistent, persevering effort.

The 10% caveat: this comes from someone who trained for international olympiads and at HRT, with very high raw intelligence. The advice doesn't apply to everyone. Not everyone has the perseverance to train themselves into long hours, or the intelligence and self-awareness to get smarter just by grinding more. For someone like Jeff, grinding feeds directly into his learning loop, so he grinds less and works smarter the next time around. For others, not necessarily. Some people need to be told to be strategic, to optimize their systems before they start, or they'll spend five hours on something that should take one, over and over.

For people with high self-awareness and constant reflection, getting smarter as experience accumulates is a built-in feature you barely notice. For others it's a muscle that needs reminding, otherwise the wasted time and energy is pure opportunity cost.

text:
I'm now building an "improvements" feature into all of my personal vibecoded applications: a freeform text input that's hooked up to an agent that yolo implements whatever is submitted.

It's an interesting experience -- the activation energy barrier to sanding any rough edge or implementing any new feature becomes extremely low. Someone else who uses one of the applications I created has already implemented 150 improvements over the course of a few days. This pattern feels like a new kind of tool -- liquid software? -- and every application that doesn't have this feature now has a slightly rigid and anachronistic flavor. Why can't I just tell it how I want it to be different?

Now, it's not obvious to me how this pattern can or should scale. Does it become unmaintainable after a while? (Maybe model intelligence improvement outstrips my feature appetite such that it's fine?) How does collaborative software work in this model? Can software designed this way be secure and reliable?

Whatever the larger questions about broader deployment, it definitely works great in a personal context. It reminds me a little of the visions of Lisp/Lisp machines, Smalltalk, and HyperCard -- systems that the user can take control of and modify. Those visions never quite worked, though: the vast majority of software today is not end-user modifiable in any useful way. So, while this "liquid" affordance is a very small touch, the way it changes one's relation to the software feels a bit transgressive and empowering in a Lickliderian and Engelbartian way.

text:
Technology has mostly been built around durable yet centralized trust systems. But the factors acting against these systems are getting more powerful as we near Super Intelligence™️. 

Obviously code can break due to the sheer mathematical progress AI is bringing, but less obviously, humans can be broken too. Impersonation, blackmail, and other forms of social engineering attacks are only going to get more advanced. As such, just fixing holes in code made to secure our lives is not enough, to build truly trustworthy systems of value, you will have to decentralize them and add immutability such that no single actor can, in most clear words, “not fuck it up.” This is exactly what Ethereum was built for. 

“Alright man, so what is Ethereum doing to survive this age? Are we cooked?”

Quite the contrary, the frontier is moving fast, but Ethereum is moving faster. Some quick points: 

1. The Hegotá upgrade will set the tone. 

This upgrade will make Ethereum cryptographically agile. 

EIP-8141, lovingly known as “Frames,” changes Ethereum accounts at the root level so that transaction validations can be programmable instead of tied to the ECSDA key (the thing Justin is warning people about in his post). Essentially accounts can choose how to authenticate instead of being tied to the current status quo. There are a few quantum proof signatures out there like ML-DSA and SPHINCS, with frames you can choose whatever and also be open to even more gigabrain ones to come. When you are faced with a threat, agility is key, and Hegotá sets the tone for that agility.

2. The J* upgrade will produce a MVP quantum proof L1. 

Okay, I know what you’re thinking, “why would you ever name such a consequential thing ‘I*’???What is wrong with you??” Trust me I thought this too, but I was promptly educated that names are not finalized until we get closer, in fact, the names even get a fun emoji next to them (e.g The Hegotá upgrade emoji is a goat 🐐 IFYKYK :P)

ANYWAYS

Think of J* as answering “what are the minimal changes Ethereum needs to make if quantum computers exist tomorrow?”  

The goal here is to have enough to survive Q-day. Today, this maps to achieving a PQ heartbeat on consenus layers, leanDA PQ sampling, and leanSPHINCS transactions on execution. 

TLDR: the aim is to ship this and then play Alright by Kendrick shortly after: “we gon’ be alright!” 

4. The boxes are moving in real time 

If you’ve ever seen the strawmap (a proposed roadmap for Ethereum), you’ll know it has a lot of boxes. In particular, there is a quantum box. Also fun fact: it’s literally called a strawmap because it moves as research moves, and man is it moving! 

> On August 12, leanVM was moved forward from J* to I*
> A week later, the roadmap added the minimal viable post-quantum L1 milestone to J* 

If you’re ever wondering whether Ethereum is taking this seriously, just watch the boxes and see how they dance. 

5. AI is actually HELPING

AI makes cryptographic research faster, and AI assisted formal verification means you don’t have to trust AI’s answer. Check out some of @fradamt’s posts for more. 

6. Quantum is just one threat in a much bigger battle 

You can quantum proof a bank’s system but still be fallible to the humans that run it. Ethereum tackles this from both sides, it gardens the security while also distributing the authors of the network such that there is no single point of attack.

Other blockchains, and any place that stores value TBH, will begin to claim they are quantum proof, but they fail to address the threat of being human proof too. 

7. The grand prize is here, and Ethereum can grab it. 

A neutral and secure place for ALL value, that cannot be coerced by a government, a company, or Superintelligence. 

Your life, your story, your money, can be here, forever. And many generations from now, the kids will look up and think: thank god they tried. 

Godspeed. 

Ethereum.
